# How to Improve LLM Accuracy Without Retraining Your Entire Model

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Sep 28, 2026

·

11min read

When a model starts making mistakes in production, the instinct is to retrain it.

A full retrain is slow, expensive, and often solves the wrong problem. Most accuracy issues trace back to one of two places: the model lacks information it needs, or it behaves inconsistently with information it already has. Only the second one is really about the model itself, and even then, a full retrain is rarely the first or best lever to pull.

This article walks through four ways to raise LLM accuracy without retraining the entire model: prompt and context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, lightweight fine-tuning, and continual data updates.

### Diagnose the Problem Before You Reach for a Fix

Before choosing a technique, it helps to know which of two problems is causing bad output: context or behavior. If it’s context, that means the model doesn't have the information it needs, because that information wasn't in its training data, is out of date, or is proprietary. A behavior problem, on the other hand, means the model has the right information but still produces inconsistent formatting, tone, or reasoning.

There's a second reason this matters. Some accuracy gaps are one-time and can be patched. Others keep reopening as the underlying facts or edge cases change, and patching them individually stops working after a while. [Continual learning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-continual-learning) is built to fix this (and we'll come back to it).

### Prompt and Context Engineering

Prompt and context engineering adjusts what you ask the model to do and what information you give it alongside the question, without touching the model's weights.

How it works: Add clear instructions, examples of the input and expected output, or reference text the model can pull from directly in the prompt. A structured system prompt with two or three worked examples often turns a generic, wrong answer into a correct one.

Best for: Tasks with a clear right answer where the required knowledge already lives in the model or fits comfortably in the context window, such as classification, formatting, translation, or summarization.

Trade-offs: Prompt engineering doesn't scale well once a task needs a wide range of dynamic, per-query information; a static prompt can't hold every fact a business might need, and longer prompts cost more per call. When teams hit that wall, the model usually isn't wrong about the task, it just doesn't have the right facts in front of it.
title: How to Improve LLM Accuracy Without Retraining Your Entire Model

text:
[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/improve-llm-accuracy-without-retraining | Type: blog_post | Title: How to Improve LLM Accuracy Without Retraining Your Entire Model | Published: 2026-09-28 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
The prompt itself is only part of the picture. A model's harness, the surrounding tools, context management, and delivery checks it's wired into, affects accuracy just as much as the wording of a single prompt. On a legal-agent benchmark, [Adaption's research](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/a-better-harness-can-unlock-smaller-models) found that harness changes alone, with no change to the model's weights, moved an open model's task-pass rate from 67 percent to 85 percent.

### Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, retrieves relevant information from an external source, a document store, database, or search index, and inserts it into the prompt before the model generates an answer.

How it works: A query is converted into an embedding, matched against a vector database of pre-indexed content, and the closest matches are pulled into the prompt as context. The model then answers using that retrieved material instead of relying only on what it learned during training.

Best for: Questions that depend on current, proprietary, or fast-changing information, such as product catalogs, internal documentation, recent updates, or account-specific data, that a static prompt or the model's training data can't cover.

Trade-offs: [RAG](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-continual-learning) introduces a new failure mode: retrieval quality. If the search returns the wrong documents, or too many irrelevant ones, the model can't answer correctly no matter how well it reasons, and excess noise in the context can produce hallucinations rather than prevent them. Tuning retrieval, ranking, and chunk size becomes its own ongoing project.

RAG also depends on someone having written the right information down somewhere. Adaption's research on agent memory found a related pattern: the bottleneck usually isn't retrieval at all, it's what gets extracted into memory in the first place. Improving how memory is written, before any retrieval happens, raised accuracy on long, multi-session conversations from 39 percent to 61 percent against a comparable open-source memory system; [Better Agent Memory Starts Before Retrieval](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/agent-memory-write-time) covers the full results.

### Lightweight Fine-Tuning: Adapters and Targeted Updates

Lightweight fine-tuning updates a small, targeted subset of a model's parameters, often through adapter methods like LoRA (low-rank adaptation), rather than retraining every weight in the model from scratch.

How it works: The base model stays frozen. A small number of additional parameters, sometimes under one percent of the model's total size, are trained on a focused set of examples. Because the base weights don't move, the update is faster, cheaper, and easier to reverse than a full retrain.

[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/improve-llm-accuracy-without-retraining | Type: blog_post | Title: How to Improve LLM Accuracy Without Retraining Your Entire Model | Published: 2026-09-28 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
Best for: Behavior problems. [Lightweight fine-tuning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails) teaches a model consistent tone, format, or reasoning style on a specific task where the same instruction, restated in every prompt, isn't sticking.

Trade-offs: Fine-tuning of any kind needs a representative training set. One of the most common mistakes is training on examples that don't match production conditions, such as fine-tuning on questions alone when the live system always includes retrieved context. Even a lightweight update needs infrastructure to prepare data, run training, and evaluate the result before it ships. AutoScientist automates this work, and unlike a prompt change, it can't be edited in real time. If the underlying information changes faster than the team can prepare a new training set and rerun the update, the model is out of date again almost as soon as it ships. That's the problem continual data updates are meant to solve.

### Continual Learning and Targeted Data Updates

Continual learning treats training data as something to keep improving on an ongoing basis, correcting known weak points and adding coverage for rare or newly emerging cases as they appear.

How it works: Teams identify specific gaps, such as a language with weak coverage or domain-specific edge cases, and address just that gap through a smaller, faster update cycle.

Best for: Systems where accuracy needs keep shifting, as facts change, new edge cases emerge, or coverage needs to expand into languages or use cases the original training data didn't include.

Trade-offs: This approach only works as well as the team's ability to turn a known problem into good training data, quickly and repeatedly. Without that, continual updates are just as hard to sustain as periodic retrains, only more frequent.

[Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data) and [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset) handle this. Adaptive Data improves the quality and coverage of an existing dataset. Invent a Dataset generates net-new training data from a task description, for cases like low-resource languages where no corpus exists to draw from.

### Comparing the Four Approaches

### Improving LLM Accuracy Without a Full Retrain

If eval failures point to missing or outdated information, start with prompt engineering or retrieval, and choose retrieval once that information is too large or dynamic for a static prompt. If eval failures point to inconsistent behavior on a task the model already understands, lightweight fine-tuning is usually the more direct fix. If the issue you're fixing is a recurring one, continual learning is the best fit.

Still, these approaches aren't mutually exclusive, and most production systems combine them. RAG supplies current facts, prompt engineering handles formatting and instructions, and a lightweight fine-tune or continual data refresh addresses behavior that drifts as the underlying data changes. A team might start with prompt engineering to establish a baseline and a solid evaluation set, add retrieval once the required knowledge base outgrows the context window, and add a targeted fine-tune or continual learning loop once evaluations show a specific, recurring behavior problem that more context doesn't fix.

# The True Cost of Bad Training Data (And How to Fix It)

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Sep 28, 2026

·

9min read

Most AI budgets have a line for compute and a line for annotation. Almost none have a line for what happens when the training data is wrong. That's because the cost usually doesn't show up right away. It shows up months later, and by then it doesn't look like a data problem at all.

Here's the usual sequence: a model underperforms in production. The team checks the architecture. Then the hyperparameters. Then the evaluation setup. Weeks go by before anyone checks the data itself. Once they do, the annotation budget looks small next to the cost of everything it took to find the real cause.

This article covers three things: what bad training data actually is, what it costs, and what changes when a team maintains its data instead of building it once and moving on.

### What Is Bad Training Data?

Bad training data is data that doesn't accurately represent what you're asking the model to learn. That happens in four main ways:

- Inconsistent labels: two annotators label the same example differently, and no one checks whether they agree
- Coverage gaps: whole parts of the real world are missing from the dataset, such as a language, demographic, or edge case, because they were harder to collect.
- Bias: the data reflects the world unevenly, so the model repeats that imbalance at scale.
- Staleness: the data was accurate when it was collected, but the product, users, or language changed and the dataset didn't.

Most annotation guides focus on the first three. The fourth gets skipped, even though it's often the real cause.

### The Direct Costs of Bad Training Data

Some costs are visible on a budget review. Three tend to show up first: the compute spent training on flawed data, the labor spent rebuilding the dataset once the problem is found, and the engineering time spent looking everywhere except the data itself before anyone checks it.

### Wasted Compute

Training a model on a noisy dataset and discovering the problem at evaluation means paying for the same compute twice: once for the run that failed, and again for the retrain once the dataset is fixed. At the scale of a production dataset, even a small error rate in the training data becomes thousands of flawed examples training the model directly.

### Re-annotation

Rebuilding a dataset is never just the labeling labor. It includes the audit to find the root cause, the revised guidelines, a new quality pass, and the project management overhead of running the whole process again, usually against a tighter deadline because the original one already passed.

### Misdirected Engineering Time
title: The True Cost of Bad Training Data (And How to Fix It)

text:
[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data | Type: blog_post | Title: The True Cost of Bad Training Data (And How to Fix It) | Published: 2026-09-28 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
When a model underperforms, the instinct is to check its architecture, hyperparameters, and the training procedure first. Data is often the last thing anyone examines, which means the single most expensive line item in a bad-data incident is the weeks of senior engineering time spent ruling out everything else first.

While these three costs tend to show up first, they're the smaller share of the total, and the easiest to catch. The ones that cost the most never show up as a line item.

### The Hidden Costs of Bad Training Data

These are harder to price, and they're often where bad training data costs the most.

A model trained on flawed data is usually evaluated against a test set with the same flaws. The evaluation passes. The failure only shows up once real users send inputs the training data never covered, and by then it's public, not internal.

A dataset rebuild that delays a launch by a quarter costs more than that quarter. It can cost the market position to whichever competitor ships first, and that loss never shows up in the annotation budget's postmortem.

The [EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/) and similar frameworks now expect documented data provenance, not just a working model. Retrofitting that documentation onto a dataset built without an audit trail costs more than building it in from the start.

Technical debt compounds beneath it all. Code debt is visible in a codebase. Data debt is not. Teams build models on the flawed dataset, then products on those models, then customer workflows on those products. Fixing the root cause later means touching every layer built on top of it.

None of these costs appear on the annotation line item. All of them get charged to the AI program anyway.

### Why Better Annotation Doesn't Fix Staleness

Most guidance on the cost of bad training data ends with a vendor recommendation: better annotators, tighter quality checks, more careful guidelines. All of that helps with the first three patterns described above. None of it addresses staleness, because a dataset can pass every quality check the day it ships and still be wrong six months later, once the world it was built to represent has moved on.

Something has to [keep a model's inputs current as conditions change](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-continual-learning), rather than assuming a dataset built once will still hold up later. That's the space most AI systems are missing, and it's a different problem from annotation quality. Annotation quality asks whether the data was right when it was collected. Staleness asks whether it's still right now.

### How to Fix Bad Training Data

Each of the four patterns calls for a different fix. Some are procedural. Some need a dataset that keeps working after the model ships.

### Inconsistent Labels
title: The True Cost of Bad Training Data (And How to Fix It)

text:
[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data | Type: blog_post | Title: The True Cost of Bad Training Data (And How to Fix It) | Published: 2026-09-28 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
The fix here is well established: guidelines that are tested and versioned before work begins, annotators trained and calibrated against a gold panel in the relevant domain, agreement between annotators measured on an ongoing basis rather than assumed, and documented provenance so a dataset can survive a regulator's or a model-risk team's review. Skipping any of these to save time up front reliably costs more later.

### Coverage Gaps

Closing a coverage gap starts with finding it. An audit that checks representation across languages, demographics, and edge cases before training begins catches most of them. But some gaps exist because the data was never collected at all. [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-invent-a-dataset) is built for that case. It generates a dataset from a description of the task, useful for a low-resource language or a new task type where no corpus exists to draw from.

### Bias

This one is closer to a discipline than a tool. The fix is deliberately checking who and what the data represents, against the population the model will serve, rather than assuming a large enough dataset averages out on its own. This is an ongoing check that someone owns.

### Staleness

Staleness is not a one-time deliverable to fix. It requires ongoing monitoring: watching for drift between what the model sees in production and what it was trained on, and closing gaps as they appear. [Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/adaption-launches-adaptive-data-beta) treats this as [continuous work](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-continual-learning), improving quality and surfacing long-tail examples a static dataset tends to miss. In early deployments, Adaption has reported an 82 percent average increase in data quality and support across 242 languages, the kind of coverage that's difficult to reach when adding a language means restarting a manual curation project from zero.

### Treat Datasets as Infrastructure

Organizations that get their data right don't treat it as a one-time delivery. They keep auditing for coverage gaps, checking for bias, and monitoring for drift. That protects everything downstream: compute, engineering time, launch timelines, and regulatory exposure. Everything depends on the dataset staying accurate after it ships.

Adaption released [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-invent-a-dataset), which generates a high-quality AI-ready training dataset based on a user’s description and requested volume. Going from a dataset description to a dataset that captures a capability is one of the hardest agentic tasks. Typically, a core issue is diversity collapse as the volume of data requested expands. It is also hard to preserve the quality of data generations at scale.

To assess progress in the zero-data regime, we evaluate [Invent API](https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/invent-a-dataset/) alongside APIs from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Zai for of a variety of dataset requests covering different tasks, domains, and languages, at sizes ranging from 200 to 20,000 samples. In contrast, Invent explicitly permits commercial use for downstream training. We also include open-weight models as a feasible alternative.

Invent API produces the most diverse and highest-quality datasets, with training datasets 19%-55% more diverse than every model tested. Crucially, Invent’s diversity advantage does not come at a quality cost, it is pareto-frontier, improving on both objectives at once. It also outperforms on quality, about 17% higher than the strongest baselines, Claude Opus 5 and GLM-5.3\. That means, with Invent API, you can generate as much data as a project needs, without hitting a point where more data means worse data.

Most teams start a new capability with no data. Invent a Dataset turns a single description into training data that maintains quality and diversity as it grows, so teams can build the capabilities they want without waiting for a dataset to exist.

# Automated Data Quality Control With Agentic Checklists

[Wei-Yin Ko](https://www.linkedin.com/in/wei-yin-k-7394bb42/)

 &

[Sara Hooker](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sararosehooker/)

·

Oct 08, 2026

·

7min read

Bad training data can leave a model worse off than no training at all. Catching it often means a person reading through the dataset manually, which stops being practical at tens of thousands of examples. It is harder still in domains like medicine, law, and business, where there is no single correct answer to check a response against.

New research introduces agentic checklist generation, a method in which an AI agent autonomously writes the quality checks itself. It builds a checklist from past runs of [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist), Adaption's automated training system, then uses it to filter training data automatically.

In domains with no single correct answer, criteria have traditionally been designed and enforced by hand. Our agentic checklist generates verifiable requirements for these otherwise unverifiable domains instead.

In testing, models trained on 10,000 checklist-filtered examples had relative win rates 9.4% to 13.2% higher than models trained on 10,000 randomly sampled ones. The result held across general, medical, legal, and technology domains.

### A Checklist Built by an Agent With Minimal Human Input

No single definition of "good data" works across the 44 expert domains AutoScientist supports. Each domain has its own rules and specifications for quality, so automated checks have to be domain-specific to be useful. An agentic checklist handles this by replacing the vague question "is this example good?" with specific yes-or-no questions, each tagged to the domains where it applies, so low-quality data can be found and removed before training.

Checklists for verifying datasets are not new. The novelty of our system lies in the fact that the list is written and updated by an agent with minimal human input. We use a Discovery Agent to review past AutoScientist training runs and identify critiques. From those critiques, it detects new and specific requirements for data quality across diverse domains, builds them into a checklist, and uses that checklist to filter training data automatically. A person can review the list, but does not have to.

Every AutoScientist run adds new critiques for the agent to learn from. Discovery can run continuously as experiments accumulate, and each pass produces a new version of the checklist that builds on the previous one, so coverage and specificity grow over time.

The agent tags each requirement by the domains it applies to and by difficulty, from easy to hard. Because many critiques make the same point, a compaction pass merges similar requirements when the merge adds detail, such as a specific example, and drops redundant ones.

### Prompt and Completion Quality Checklist

### The Checklist Removes Any Example That Misses a Requirement

The checklist runs as part of [Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data), Adaption's real-time data optimization platform, which optimizes, expands, and generates AI training data. A verification agent applies the checklist in two steps. It first decides which requirements apply to an example, since a rule about medical terminology has no bearing on a business email, then checks whether the example meets each one. The agent runs in reasoning mode, which the research found necessary for it to judge relevance correctly.

Any example that misses an applicable requirement is removed. A miss is a clear error, and in supervised fine-tuning, where a model learns from examples, training on an erroneous example is worse than skipping it.

The remaining examples are scored by how many requirements they meet, the more fulfilled requirements means that the example exhibits more positive traits that the past judge critiques explicitly evaluated upon. Because the number of applicable requirements differs by domain, scores are compared within each domain, and a cutoff is tuned per domain to balance quality against how much data is kept.

Given that we need the full capability of a reasoning model to utilize the checklist effectively, efficiency is an important consideration. To increase efficiency, each of the examples evaluated upon is tagged with a primary domain and only the general requirements plus the requirements with the same tagged domain from the full checklist are considered.

### Removing Low-Scoring Data Improved Win Rates

The first experiment asks what happens when the checklist removes a dataset's low-quality data and the model trains on less. It started with 50,000 examples each in medical and corporate business. We fine-tuned Gemma4-31B with LoRA twice, using a separate instance from the Discovery Agent: once on all of the data and once on what remained after the lowest-scoring 30% was removed. The training settings were held constant, so any difference comes from the data. The filtered datasets held 38,040 medical examples and 27,486 corporate business examples.

Averaged across 10 runs, the relative win rates for medical domain against the original model improved 12.1%, and for corporate business domain win rate improved 8% .

### At a Fixed Data Size, Filtering Beat Random Selection

The second experiment asks what happens when the data size stays the same and the data is the highest quality available for that size.

Llama3.3-70B was fine-tuned on 10,000 examples for each of the general, medical, legal, and technology domains. In each domain, one set was sampled randomly from a pool of 70,000 examples, and the other came from the same pool after checklist filtering. Training settings were again fixed without optimization, so the results reflect data quality alone.

Models trained on each set were scored on win rate against the original model, using the domain-specific test sets from the AutoScientist Leaderboard, which collect the most challenging tasks on Adaption's platform for each domain. Training on checklist-filtered data outperformed random selection in every domain. The gains are relative, meaning the improvement as a share of the random-sample model's win rate: 11.4% in general, 10.1% in medical, 9.4% in legal, and 13.2% in technology.

Win rates of models trained on randomly sampled versus checklist-filtered data across 10 runs by domain.

Relative win-rate gain of models trained on checklist-filtered data over models trained on randomly sampled data.

Across both experiments, filtering with the checklist improved average win rates in every domain tested. That suggests the agent finds requirements that separate good data from bad with minimal human input.

### What Becomes Possible When Quality Checks Learn

Reliable gains in AI increasingly come from curating data and improving training technique rather than adding scale. Curation depends on a standard for what good data looks like, and a standard that learns from use does not have to be rewritten as the work changes. It follows the work.

That matters most where there is no answer key. In domains like medicine, law, and business, the standard for good data can't be looked up. It has to be learned. This checklist learns from every run.

Intelligence that adapts starts with data that does too.

# What Is Adaptive AI? How Systems That Learn and Adjust Work

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Oct 09, 2026

·

9min read

Adaptive AI is an artificial intelligence framework that autonomously learns from and adjusts to environmental changes during live deployment. Rather than relying on frozen model configurations, adaptive systems continuously optimize their behavior in real time, with the user’s objective, not raw model scale, as the focus.

### How Does Adaptive AI Differ From Traditional AI?

Traditional artificial intelligence is model-centric. That means it prioritizes shipping large, general foundational models optimized for no one. Adaptive AI, on the other hand, is strictly task-centric. The focus is on smaller models built around your objective.

Traditional AI’s brute-force scaling method creates a locked snapshot after deployment. To get traditional models to fit your needs, you end up with constant prompt rewriting (also known as the “prompt engineering tax”) or workflows contorted around software limitations.

Adaptive AI stands against this scale-at-all-costs approach. It adapts to your language, culture, and regulatory requirements, and it adjusts how much compute it uses to the difficulty of the task.

### Adaptive AI vs Traditional AI

|                 | Traditional AI                                  | Adaptive AI                                     |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Post Deployment | Model stays fixed until retrained               | Behavior updates during live use                |
| Growth Strategy | Larger models, more data, more compute          | Lower cost of adjusting to each task            |
| Core Structure  | Model-centric: one general model for every user | Task-centric: built around the user’s objective |
| Learning Method | Gradient-based retraining                       | Inference-time, gradient-free adjustments       |
| Data Layer      | Assembled once, updated slowly                  | Generated and improved as objectives change     |

### What Are The Key Characteristics Of Adaptive AI?

Adaptive AI is characterized by three core structural pillars: task-centricity, [continuous learning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-continual-learning) during live use, and an architecture built around dynamic post-training and adaptive inference. These design choices ensure intelligence doesn’t arrive preconfigured, but develops through direct interaction with the world.

The foundational design prioritizes task outcomes over the raw scale of model parameters. Models trained on a global average of the internet underserve rare cases, regional languages, and specialized industries, because they are built for general use. A task-centric system adjusts to different languages, industries, and specialized operations instead.

### How Does Adaptive AI Learn And Improve In Real Time?

Today’s AI paradigm is backward because it treats live software as a frozen snapshot. A traditional model lacks the internal mechanics to absorb real-time corrections, so it repeats the same operational errors until developers intervene with an expensive, manual retraining patch. Adaption co-founder and CEO Sara Hooker [describes the problem](https://observer.com/2026/02/sara-hooker-raises-50m-to-challenge-a-i-s-conventional-wisdom-interview/) this way: after release, “user feedback is lost in a vacuum.”

Adaptive architecture resolves this by separating long-term parametric weights from immediate test-time memory adjustments. When a user interacts with the system or inputs a correction, the inference layer captures this feedback signal and updates its context parameters instantly. This dual-storage mechanism lets the application change its routing paths on the fly and learn directly from production experience. Hooker points to the brain as the model: short-term and long-term memory are stored separately, and she calls building that dual storage into algorithms one of the most interesting questions ahead.

Adaptive architecture resolves this by separating long-term parametric weights from immediate test-time memory adjustments. When a user interacts with the system or inputs a correction, the inference layer captures this feedback signal and updates its context parameters instantly.

Hooker [draws on how the brain stores](https://x.com/sarahookr/status/2048759884125233453) short-term and long-term memory separately, and calls building that dual storage into algorithms one of the most interesting questions ahead. This dual-storage mechanism allows the application to alter its routing paths on the fly, mimicking human intelligence by learning directly from production experience.

### How Does Adaptive AI Work Without Expensive Retraining?

Live behavioral shifts occur through inference-time, gradient-free techniques that sit directly above foundation models as a functional algorithmic layer. This separation allows organizations to combine, route, and improve model behaviors instantly without triggering massive data processing costs. Researchers call adjusting a trained model to new data at inference time [test-time adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03687). Many methods still update model weights, and [recent research](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2604.13552.md) shows they can do so without gradients.

Standard retraining and fine-tuning require gradient descent, which updates the model’s core weights at significant compute cost. Non-technical builders can think of gradient-free adaptation as a way to change system outputs without altering the underlying model’s permanent core weights. By applying these techniques at the inference stage, everyday builders can get continual learning without runaway compute bills.

### How Does Adaptive AI Treat Data?

Standard AI development treats a dataset as an expensive, one-time collection, finished once it’s assembled. Real-world conditions and enterprise workflows change constantly, so a fixed dataset falls out of line with live operating conditions, and models can become less accurate as time passes since their last training cycle. Adaptive Data, part of the Adaption platform, makes the data space malleable. Builders can raise data quality and add rare long-tail examples. When no data exists to start from, Invent a Dataset generates a dataset from a description of the task. Both give builders practical control over their data, so they can keep updating it as objectives change and new edge cases appear in production.

### What Does Task-Centric AI Mean For Users?

Transitioning from a model-centric design to a task-centric framework removes the operational friction that companies face during deployment, altering three clear areas of the everyday user experience.

### Eliminating the Prompt Engineering Tax

The user no longer has to write hyper-specific prompts or guess the right context to get a useful response from a frozen system. The application evaluates the intent behind the objective and configures its own compute allocation to achieve the target outcome.

### True Local Customization

Traditional models fail to capture regional nuances because they are built on global averages. Task-centric architectures naturally adapt to the native language, culture, and localized regulatory compliance rules of the specific enterprise workflow.

### Proportional Compute Allocation

A standard model typically spends the same compute on a simple arithmetic question as on a complex legal one. Adaptive systems scale compute proportionally to the difficulty of the goal, deploying fast micro-models for low-latency tasks and increasing thinking time for long-horizon reasoning.

### What Are Examples Of Adaptive AI?

Adaptive AI is actively deployed across specialized verticals where live accuracy is paramount.

### Automated Training Loops

The [AutoScientist platform](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist) automates the research loop behind model training by co-optimizing data curation and training recipes until performance converges on a specific objective. This automated system achieves a 35 percent relative improvement over human-configured training templates, lifting enterprise win rates on specialized tasks from 48 percent to 64 percent.

### Regional Language Generation

In large-scale localization initiatives like recent regional pilots in Singapore, developers used Adaptive Data to automatically [generate 750,000 localized training samples](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/ai-singapore-sovereign-ai-pilot) across five distinct Southeast Asian languages in a single month. This automated data loop saved engineering teams 56 hours of manual hyperparameter optimization.

### Production Micro-Models

### Why Does Adaptive AI Matter?

Enterprise work depends on specifics: local languages, regulations, and workflows that change over time. A model trained once for the average use case can’t keep up with them. When it makes a mistake in production, it repeats that mistake until developers retrain it or the team rewrites prompts to work around it.

AI that adapts removes that dependence. It takes in corrections while it’s running, adjusts to the specific objective, and uses more compute on hard tasks and less on easy ones, so cost follows the work. Progress then depends on how cost-efficiently a system adapts to the task in front of it, not on the size of a frozen model.

# The Best Way to Reduce Your Company's AI Token Spend

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

10min read

The best way to reduce your company’s AI token spend is to build your own custom model. This lets companies control cost, access, and intellectual property while reducing vendor lock-in.

### Key Takeaways:

- Company AI bills keep growing: token usage grew 1,001 percent from January 2025 to April 2026, while total spend grew 497 percent.
- Adaption co-founder Sara Hooker says costs will keep rising because token costs are artificially low, and frontier labs will have to manage margin expectations after their upcoming IPOs.
- There are two ways to reduce your company’s AI token spend: 1) adjust how you use a provider’s model or 2) build a custom model you own. Only building a custom model allows you to permanently control costs.
- Building custom models is easier with Adaption, which makes data optimization, data generation, and automated model training seamless with its Adaptive Data, Invent A Dataset, and AutoScientist platforms.

### What Is an AI Token?

An AI token is a unit of text, such as a word, word fragment, or punctuation mark, that a large language model reads or writes, and providers bill by the token. Models charge separate rates for input tokens (what you send) and output tokens (what the model returns).

### Why Do Company AI Bills Keep Growing?

Company AI bills keep growing because token usage is rising faster than per-token prices are falling. Two factors push volume up:

- Usage volume: Among businesses with connected AI accounts, Ramp found token usage grew 1,001 percent from January 2025 to April 2026, while overall spend grew 497 percent.
- Agent steps: An agent completes multi-step tasks, chooses its own tools, and decides how many steps to take, and each step is billed. A [2026 Stanford University study](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/how-do-ai-agents-spend-your-money) of eight frontier models on coding tasks found agentic tasks consumed about 1,000 times more tokens than code chat.

In an October 2026 Financial Times article on[ strategies to ](https://www.ft.com/content/3effd703-591f-43c5-828e-dd11839653eb)manage AI costs, Sara Hooker, co-founder of Adaption, which builds continual learning systems, said agentic workflows need more compute than single prompts. As a result, costs are harder to predict.

### Will AI Token Prices Fall?

Effective token prices are falling now, but they have moved in both directions, and the provider sets them. [Ramp's AI Index](https://ramp.com/data/ai-index-sept-2026) shows the effective price businesses pay per million tokens fell 41 percent, from a 2026 peak of $1.15 in March to $0.68 in early September, after providers announced price cuts.

Two further things moved the price:

- Customer trade-down. Frontier models' share of tokens fell from a 53 percent peak in August to 45 percent as some businesses set defaults toward standard models.
- Launch-driven increases. [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/09/09/ai-compute-tokens-cheaper-boom/) reported that effective prices rose after major model launches this year before easing.

Hooker expects token usage to keep growing and prices to rise, in part because the planned IPOs of frontier labs will pressure their margins. She told the Financial Times, “There’s a clear understanding in the industry that tokens are not priced properly right now. Once the IPOs \[of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic\] happen, there is going to be immediate pressure on those margins to be more sensible.”

A custom model's running cost follows its own size and hosting, so a provider's repricing in either direction does not change it. Falling prices do raise the monthly token spend a workload needs before a custom model repays its training and hosting costs.

### What Are Your Options for Reducing Token Spend?

There are two mechanisms for reducing token spend: adjust how you use a provider’s models or build your own custom model. Making adjustments lowers the number of tokens you use or the price you pay per token, but is not predictable. Only building a custom model gives you total control over AI spending.

### What Is a Custom AI Model?

A custom AI model is a model trained on a company’s proprietary data to do the work your company actually does, such as extracting clauses from contracts, classifying customer requests, or processing records in bulk. It replaces a general-purpose model with one built for a defined set of tasks. [Fine-tuning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails), which trains an existing model on new data, is one common way to build one.

### Comparison: General-Purpose Model vs Custom Model Costs

|                      | General-purpose model through an API                    | Custom model                                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| What you pay for     | Tokens at the provider's price                          | Training, then the compute to run the model     |
| Who sets the price   | The provider                                            | You and your hosting provider                   |
| Scope                | A broad range of tasks                                  | One defined set of tasks                        |
| Setup                | An API key                                              | Training data, training, and testing            |
| Where your data goes | To the provider with each request, under its data terms | Stays in your environment if you host the model |

### Why Does a Custom AI Model Cost Less to Run?

A custom model costs less to run because each request needs less compute, and the company stops paying a provider’s per-token price for work that does not need a large model. Three things drive the difference:

- Less compute per token. A model built for one set of tasks can have far fewer parameters than a general-purpose model, so each token takes less compute to process.
- A cost you set. Instead of a provider’s price list, the company pays for hosting compute, which follows model size, volume, and hardware. A provider’s repricing does not change it.
- Shorter requests. Behavior trained into the model can replace long instructions that otherwise travel with every request, which cuts input tokens.

Model choice moves cost a lot. [Ramp](https://ramp.com/blog/ai-token-cost-for-businesses) observed a 20-times difference in effective price per million tokens between the lowest-cost and a premium model in April 2026.

A smaller model can still do routine work well. In Adaption’s [September 2026 research](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/a-better-harness-can-unlock-smaller-models), A Better Harness Can Unlock Smaller Models, changing only the agent harness raised Qwen3.6-27B’s criterion pass rate on the Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark from 67.10 percent to 85.92 percent across 140 held-out tasks, with the model’s weights unchanged. Post-training then raised it to 88.03 percent, close to frontier performance on this benchmark. Most of the gain came from the harness, with post-training adding about two percentage points.

In the [July 2026 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08938), Better Harnesses, Smaller Models: Building 90% Cheaper Agents via Automated Harness Adaptation, researchers found related results across seven business tasks: in one case, a small model with an optimized harness recovered 89.7 percent of a large model’s performance at 4 percent of the cost.

On routine work, the choice is not between a large model you don’t own or a weak one you do. A smaller model can work reliably well at a fraction of the cost.

### Which Workloads Are Worth Moving to a Custom Model?

Move a workload to a custom model when it is routine, the volume is steady and high, training examples exist or can be generated, and you can test quality. Four questions to consider:

1. Is the work routine and well-defined? Bulk extraction, classification, summarizing to a set standard, policy checks, contract clause extraction, and resume parsing all fit.
2. Is the volume steady and high? Compare the workflow’s monthly token spend with the one-time cost to train a model plus the monthly cost to host and maintain it.
3. Do you have training examples? A model is only as good as its data. If you have internal data, such as logged requests paired with approved outputs or corrections to an agent’s past mistakes, the [Adaptive Data platform](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data), Adaption’s real-time data optimization platform, optimizes, expands, and generates AI training data across 242 languages and localizations, so your data is ready to train on. If you have no data, [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset), Adaption’s synthetic dataset generation platform, builds a training-ready dataset from a description of the behavior a model should learn, with no example data needed.
4. Can you test quality? A test set of real requests with a pass mark set before training makes the comparison fair, and it shows whether errors come from the model or from the tools and context around it. Check the setup before concluding a model is too weak, and keep the larger model where the remaining errors reflect capability limits.

Each step of the build has a product behind it. The Adaptive Data platform prepares the data a company already has, Invent a Dataset creates data where none exists, and AutoScientist runs the research loop that turns that data into a model the company owns. Because each step feeds the next, a team moves from a workload to a tested, owned model with fewer handoffs and less specialist effort. ### How Do You Reduce Token Spend if You Don’t Build A Custom Model?

Six options lower spend on the models a company already pays for. Each lowers the tokens used or the price per token and leaves the provider's pricing and terms in place.

### Track Spend by Workflow

Token spend tracking records the tokens each workflow, team, and model uses and what they cost. It lowers nothing by itself, but it shows which workflows drive the bill. Provider reports arrive after the fact, so a looping agent can run up cost before anyone sees it.

### Trimming Prompts, Context, and Output

Trimming removes content the model does not need and limits how much it writes back. Tokens concentrate in the system prompt, retrieved documents, chat history, and answer length. Send only what the task needs, request short structured output when software reads the result, and use ordinary code for fixed tasks such as reading a date from a field. Cutting a needed instruction can lower quality, and prompts grow back as teams add instructions.

### Routing Tasks to Smaller Models

Model routing sends each request to the lowest-cost model that does the job well: classification or formatting goes to a smaller model, and hard work goes to a premium one. Routing saves money only when the smaller model passes your quality tests, so it needs a test set of real requests and a pass mark for each task. The router is another system to re-test when prices, models, or tasks change, and every request still pays the provider's price per token.

### Caching Repeated Prompt Content

Prompt caching is a provider feature that stores the processed beginning of a prompt and charges less when a later request repeats it. Putting the system prompt, tool definitions, and reference documents first and the changing part last gives the cache something to reuse. Cache reads cost a fraction of the standard input price, and the discount varies by provider.

Caching helps only when many requests share a long, stable beginning, and workflows where every input is new get little benefit. The cache also expires, so requests that arrive far apart miss it. Caching lowers the price of repeated input only, not output, and you still depend on the provider’s pricing.

### Batching Non-Urgent Work

Batch processing submits a group of requests together and returns results later at a lower price. Frontier model providers often charge 50 percent of standard prices for batch jobs, but results can take up to 24 hours, so batching suits work that can wait, such as nightly summaries or evaluation runs. It also has restrictions: some providers do not support streaming, and zero data retention may not apply to batch jobs, which matters for companies with strict data rules. The discount is a fixed percentage off the provider’s price, so the provider still sets the price.

### Capping Agent Runs

Capping agent runs sets a limit on the steps and tokens each run can use, plus a spending limit for each team that runs agents. Each step is billed and the agent chooses how many to take, so a cap stops a looping agent early. Caps control the worst case, not the average: an agent under the cap can still waste tokens on every run, a cap set too low cuts off legitimate long tasks, and a cap set too high does little. Choosing a cap requires knowing how many steps a normal run takes.

### What Is The Best Way To Reduce Your Company’s AI Token Spend?

For routine, high-volume work, building a custom model is the best way to reduce your company’s AI token spend, because it gives you complete control over your costs. Other strategies, like capping agent runs or batching non-urgent requests can help on workloads that stay on a general model, but your company is still at mercy to a provider’s pricing and terms. A custom model changes the terms themselves, and Adaption makes this path practical.

### What Is Fine-Tuning?

[Fine-tuning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-continual-learning), also called model customization, is a training process that continues training a pretrained AI model on an organization’s own examples so the model performs a specific task more reliably. Three training methods are common:

- Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): Trains on input and output pairs that show the desired response
- Direct preference optimization (DPO): Trains on pairs of preferred and rejected responses
- Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT): Trains on a reward function that scores each output the model generates

Each method can update a small set of adapter weights, known as LoRA (low-rank adaptation), or every weight in the model, known as full fine-tuning.

### What Is LLM Fine-Tuning?

- Lower cost. Training replaces long prompts, so token spend per call drops, and a smaller trained model can replace a large proprietary one for a specific task.

Synthetic data is artificial data generated by rules, simulations, statistical models, or generative AI rather than collected from real-world events. Teams use it to train and test machine learning models when real data is scarce, private, or costly to label. Its value depends on how it is generated, checked, and mixed with real data.

### Key Takeaways

- Synthetic data types differ in how much real data they keep: fully synthetic data keeps none, partially synthetic data replaces sensitive values in a real dataset, and hybrid data pairs real records with generated ones.
- Specification-based generation builds a synthetic dataset from a description of the behavior a model should learn, so a team with no example data for a capability can still start.
- Provider terms can restrict what a team does with generated data, because some frontier model providers do not permit training on data generated with their models.

### What Is Synthetic Data?

Synthetic data, also called artificial data, is data produced by rules, simulations, statistical models, or generative AI rather than observed in the real world. Synthesizing data means generating new records that follow the structure and patterns of the cases they represent, such as a card transaction or a patient question. A synthetic dataset is a collection of those records.

Synthetic data has two common roles in AI work: standing in for real data that is private or hard to obtain, and supplying training examples for capabilities that no collected data covers.

Three properties separate useful synthetic data from random values:

- Structure: records follow the format a system expects, such as table rows, chat turns, or images.
- Realism: values and relationships stay close to the cases they represent.
- Coverage: the data includes rare cases that collected data seldom contains.

### What Are the Types of Synthetic Data?

Synthetic data is classified by how much real data it contains and by its format. Fully synthetic data contains no real records, partially synthetic data replaces selected values in a real dataset, and hybrid data combines real records with generated ones.

| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Fully synthetic     | Generated records only, built to match the patterns or behavior of the cases they represent                   | Training models when no real data exists, or sharing data without real records |
| Partially synthetic | A real dataset in which sensitive values, such as names and contact details, are replaced with generated ones | Analysis that needs real structure but not real identities                     |
| Hybrid              | Real records combined with fully synthetic records                                                            | Expanding a small real dataset while keeping its real signal                   |

Synthetic data can be produced in various forms:

- Text: instruction and response pairs, conversations, and documents
- Tabular: rows and columns, such as transactions or patient records
- Images and video: rendered or generated scenes for vision models
- Time series: generated sensor readings or event sequences

### How Is Synthetic Data Generated?

Synthetic data is generated by four families of methods: rule-based simulation, statistical sampling, learned generative models, and large language model (LLM) generation. Each starts from a different input, which determines where it works and where it fails.

| Statistical sampling                                                                                          | Distributions and correlations fitted to real data | Tables and time series with well-understood structure      | Misses relationships the model does not capture |

| LLM generation                                                                                                | Prompts, seed examples, or a described behavior    | Text, such as instructions, dialogue, and preference pairs | Repetition as dataset size grows                |

### How Do Seed-Based and Specification-Based Generation Differ?

Seed-based generation expands a small pool of human-written examples, while specification-based generation starts from a description of the target behavior. Most synthetic data techniques assume a team starts with a seed pool of prompts or an existing dataset to improve, but often, teams have no example data at all.

An example of a specification-based synthetic data generator is [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset). It builds a training-ready dataset from a description of the behavior a model should learn, with no seed data, schema, or labeling guide. A team describes a task, such as summarizing business documents to an organization’s standards or classifying customer requests across departments, and sets dataset size and scope in the same flow.

### Why Does Synthetic Data Matter for AI?

Synthetic data matters for AI because the quality of a model’s output is dependent on the quality of the data it is trained on. Often, the data a team needs does not exist, cannot be shared, or costs too much to label. Synthetic data AI workflows address three constraints:

- Scarcity: rare events such as fraud, uncommon conditions, and edge cases appear too seldom in collected data, and generation can add them on demand.
- Privacy: teams can develop and share data that holds no real customer or patient records.
- Labeling cost: generated examples arrive with labels or completions attached, which reduces manual annotation.

Customization is the larger reason many organizations use synthetic training data. General-purpose models are built for broad use, and a company’s own policies, tone, and workflows rarely appear in public data in the form a model needs. Synthetic data lets a team specify that behavior directly. A bank can describe how it reviews a disputed charge, a health system can describe its intake protocols, and a law firm can specify the jurisdictions it practices in.

### What Is Synthetic Data Used For?

Synthetic data is used wherever real data is rare, restricted, or expensive to label, including fraud detection, clinical research, vehicle safety testing, manufacturing inspection, software testing, and language model training.

| Finance                 | Suspicious transaction patterns and risk scenarios                                    | Fraud examples are rare in collected data                  |
| Healthcare              | Patient records, clinical question-and-answer pairs, and medical images               | Records are private, and rare conditions have few examples |
| Automotive              | Driving scenes and crash scenarios                                                    | Real crash data is costly and dangerous to collect         |
| Manufacturing           | Defect images and sensor readings                                                     | Defects occur too seldom to photograph at volume           |
| Software testing        | Realistic records for development and performance tests                               | Developers can work without access to personal data        |
| Language model training | Instruction and response pairs, dialogue, preference pairs, and multilingual examples | Needed behaviors are missing from collected data           |

### How Is Synthetic Data Different From Real, Anonymized, and Simulated Data?

Synthetic data differs from real data in origin, from anonymized data in content, and from simulated data in scope, since simulation is one method of producing synthetic data.

### What Are the Risks of Synthetic Data?

The main risks of synthetic data are inherited bias, model collapse, privacy obligations that still apply, and unverified quality. You can reduce each through how you generate, filter, and mix the data with real data.

| Risk                | What Happens                                                   | How To Reduce It                                                      |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Inherited bias      | A generator trained on skewed records generates skewed records | Audit the generator and its source records                            |
| Model collapse      | Repeated training on model output loses rare examples          | Mix in real data and avoid training on a model’s own output in loops  |
| Privacy obligations | Personal data rules can still apply                            | Assess re-identification risk and check the applicable rules          |
| Unverified quality  | Errors and repeated patterns in the data carry into the model  | Check accuracy, duplicates, and constraint violations before training |

### What Makes Synthetic Training Data High Quality?

High-quality synthetic training data is accurate, diverse, task-relevant, and consistent with the constraints a team sets. Four checks apply:

- Accuracy: facts, labels, and completions are correct.
- Diversity: examples differ in meaning and wording, with few duplicates.
- Constraint following: length, format, tone, persona, and language match the request.
- Downstream testing: you train a model on the data and compare it with baselines on held-out prompts.

It depends on the provider’s terms. Some frontier model providers do not permit training on data generated with their models, while some open-weight model licenses do permit it, so a team should read the terms for every model it generates data with.

Three checks apply before training on generated data:

- Terms of service: confirm whether the provider allows outputs to be used to train another model.
- Model licenses: read the license of each open-weight model, because permissions differ.
- Commercial use: confirm the terms cover commercial deployment of the trained model, not only research.

The terms decide who controls the result. A dataset a team may train on commercially is an asset the team can reuse across models, while restricted terms can limit what a team does with every model trained on the data. # LLM Token Cost Optimization in 2026: Which Services Help?

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Oct 23, 2026

·

5min read

LLM token cost optimization is the practice of reducing what you pay for the tokens a language model processes by sending fewer tokens, paying less per token, or avoiding calls. Services that support it fall into five groups: provider caching and batch discounts, AI gateways, model routers, observability tools, and owned models.

### Key Takeaways

- Provider prompt caching and batch processing lower the price of repeated input and deferrable work, but neither changes the per-token price of new input.
- Gateways and routers cut the cost of individual requests: in the RouteLLM research, routers reduced cost by more than 85 percent on MT Bench while still reaching 95 percent of GPT-4's performance.
- Observability and spend-management services show which workflow, team, or model drives the bill, while leaving the provider's pricing in place.
- Owned models are the only option that changes who sets the price: they replace provider calls for the workloads they cover with your own hosting cost.

### What Is LLM Token Cost Optimization?

LLM token cost optimization is the practice of [reducing what you pay](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/reduce-company-ai-token-spend) for the tokens a language model processes, without lowering the quality of the work. Models read and write text in tokens, which are short chunks of words, and providers bill input tokens (what you send) and output tokens (what the model returns) at separate rates.

Spend is growing fast. [Menlo Ventures](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/) estimated that companies spent $37 billion on generative AI in 2025, up from $11.5 billion in 2024, and [Gartner](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-19-gartner-forecasts-worldwide-ai-spending-to-grow-47-percent-in-2026) forecasts $32.6 billion in worldwide spending on AI models in 2026, up from $15.5 billion in 2025.

The bill builds up in four places, and the services in this guide work on one or more of them:

- Resent context. Agents send history, instructions, retrieved documents, and tool definitions again on every step.
- Output length. Providers generally price output tokens above input tokens, so long responses cost more per token.
- Model choice. A premium model costs more per token than a smaller model for the same request.
- Retries and failed runs. Tokens spent on work that does not succeed still appear on the bill.

### What Should You Look for in a Token-Reduction Service?

Score every token-reduction service on the same six criteria. Together they show which part of your bill a service changes, what it puts at risk, and what it leaves with your provider.

- What it changes. The part of the bill the service acts on: fewer tokens, a lower price per token, fewer calls, better visibility into spend, or a different party setting the price.
- Quality risk. Whether the service can change the answers your users get, and how you would test that before and after adopting it.
- Coverage. Which requests the service actually sees. A gateway, for example, governs only the traffic you route through it.
- Dependence on provider pricing. Whether your savings still depend on a provider's per-token price and terms after you adopt the service.
- Vendor status and hosting. Whether you host the service yourself or buy it as a managed product, and who owns and maintains it.
- Setup effort. What your team has to change in code, data, or process before the service starts saving money.

### Do Provider Prompt Caching and Batch Discounts Reduce Token Spend?

Prompt caching lowers the price of repeated input, and batch processing lowers the price of work that can wait. As of October 2026, Anthropic and OpenAI both build prompt caching into their APIs, and Anthropic also offers batch processing at 50 percent less than standard calls.

Neither feature lowers the per-token price of new input or output. A prompt that starts differently on every call gets no caching discount, and savings depend on the hit rate, because a cached prefix expires if matching requests arrive too far apart.

### Which Services Support LLM Token Cost Optimization?

Five services lower or show what you pay a provider, and one approach changes who sets the price. As of October 2026, each entry covers what the service is, why it works, and where it falls short.

### LiteLLM

LiteLLM is an open-source AI gateway: software that sits between your applications and model providers. It applies budgets, routing, and fallbacks to every request that passes through it. You host it yourself, so your team deploys and operates the proxy and its database.

### Portkey

Portkey is a hosted AI gateway, owned by Palo Alto Networks since May 2026\. It adds caching, fallbacks, conditional routing, and budget limits to the requests you send through it. Tools that call providers directly sit outside its budgets.

### OpenRouter

OpenRouter is a hosted API that sits in front of many model providers. It sends each request to the provider that best matches your price or speed priority, and its Auto Router can pick a model for each prompt. Routing works in research: the [RouteLLM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665) reports routers cutting cost by more than 85 percent on MT Bench while still reaching 95 percent of GPT-4's performance. The catch is quality, so you need to test a cheaper model on each task.

### Helicone

Helicone is an open-source observability platform that logs requests through a proxy. It reports cost by user, session, and feature, so you can see which workflows drive spend. It doesn’t lower costs on its own, and it has been in maintenance mode since March 2026.

### Ramp Token Spend Management

Ramp Token Spend Management is a hosted service for Ramp customers. It consolidates AI spend across Anthropic, OpenAI, and other providers by model and team, flags anomalies, and offers no engineering data export. It shows and allocates spend, but cutting it still falls to the engineers who control prompts, caching, and routing.

### Build a Model You Own to Stop Depending on Provider Pricing

These five services can lower your bill, but each still pays the provider’s per-token price. If that price rises, the savings shrink.

Sara Hooker, Adaption’s co-founder and CEO, told the Financial Times in October 2026, as [quoted in Adaption’s post on token spend](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/reduce-company-ai-token-spend): “There’s a clear understanding in the industry that tokens are not priced properly right now. Once the IPOs \[of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic\] happen, there is going to be immediate pressure on those margins to be more sensible.”

The workaround is a model you own. A smaller open-weight model adapted to your routine, high-volume tasks runs on hosting you pay for, so your own hosting cost replaces the provider’s per-token price for those tasks.

[Adaption](https://adaptionlabs.ai/) is an AI company that builds continual learning systems, which let organizations train, customize, and own their AI. [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist), Adaption’s system for automating the research loop behind model training, co-optimizes a model’s training data and training recipe against an outcome the team sets. You define the task, the training examples, and the pass mark, then host the model and test it on your own requests.

Smaller models can handle routine work when the harness around them is well built. In Adaption’s September 2026 [research on the Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/a-better-harness-can-unlock-smaller-models), an optimized harness, meaning the tools, context management, execution loop, and delivery checks around a model, scored 84 percent with Qwen. That was within 0.79 percentage points of Prime Agent, with 54 percent fewer input tokens. Quality work, reduced cost.

For which workloads fit an owned model, how to build one, and AutoScientist’s measured results, see [How to Reduce Your Company’s AI Token Spend](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/reduce-company-ai-token-spend).

### How Do You Choose a Token-Reduction Service?

Choose based on your situation, and run the options in parallel instead of in sequence.

- Agents resend long, stable instructions on every call: start with provider prompt caching, which needs no new vendor.
- Work can wait up to 24 hours: use provider batch processing for jobs such as nightly summaries or evaluation runs.
- Many teams and providers need shared budgets and fallbacks: use an AI gateway such as LiteLLM or Portkey.
- Task difficulty varies, and a cheaper model passes your quality test on some tasks: use a model router such as OpenRouter.
- You cannot say which workflow drives the bill: use Helicone for engineering or Ramp Token Spend Management for finance.
- Routine, high-volume workflow: build an owned model with [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist).

You do not have to exhaust the other options before starting an owned-model project. The usual gate is data preparation and training effort, and automated data and training tools address both.

Whichever service you choose, measure cost per completed task on your own requests. A cheaper path that fails more often can raise the total bill.

# Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Oct 23, 2026

·

5min read

Real data is information recorded from actual events, people, or documents. [Synthetic data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-generation-platforms) is information generated by a model, simulation, or rules to substitute for real data. Real data serves as the accuracy reference. Synthetic data supplies volume, rare cases, and sharing without real records. Teams commonly combine both, keeping real data for evaluation.

### Key Takeaways

- Real data serves as the reference for accuracy, so a held-out real test set stays in the pipeline even when most training data is generated.
- Synthetic data adds volume, rare cases, and sharing without real records, but it reflects only what its generator learned or was told.
- Model collapse appears when models train indiscriminately on model-generated content, so what you keep matters as much as what you generate.
- Starting requirements differ by generation method: some generators need real data to learn from, and specification-based generation starts from a description of the behavior.

### How Do Synthetic Data and Real Data Differ?

[Synthetic data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-synthetic-data) and real data differ in origin, which drives their trade-offs in privacy, cost, coverage, and [fidelity](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data).
title: Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose
