|                           | Real Data                                                    | Synthetic Data                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Ground truth and fidelity | Records actual events, including noise and bias              | Matches real data only as closely as the generator learned it, so fidelity varies by method and has to be tested    |
| Privacy                   | Can contain personal records, and access is often restricted | Can avoid real records, but privacy obligations can still apply, so test re-identification risk                     |
| Cost structure            | Collection, cleaning, and labeling costs grow with volume    | Low cost per example once a generator exists, with cost moving to building and validating it                        |
| Rare-case coverage        | Limited to what was recorded                                 | Can target rare cases on demand, within what the generator can produce                                              |
| Role in evaluation        | Reference for held-out test sets                             | Useful for training and stress tests, with results checked against real data                                        |
| Starting requirement      | Access to the source records                                 | Depends on the method: some generators need real data, and others start from a description                          |
| Permitted use             | Governed by consent, licenses, and privacy rules             | Governed by the terms of the model or tool that generated it, and some providers restrict training on their outputs |

### What Is Real Data?

Real data is information collected from actual events, people, instruments, or documents, such as customer chats, sensor readings, transactions, and scanned records. Real data is the reference for what happened and for whether a model is right, but it also carries the noise, gaps, and sampling bias of the world.

### Strengths of Real Data

- It shows the true distribution, including the rare cases that occurred.
- It supplies the held-out test set that every other kind of data is checked against.
- It carries the wording, dialect, and domain detail of real users.

### Limits of Real Data

- Collection bias: real data over-represents what was easy to record.
- Gaps and label noise: fields go missing, labels conflict, and old scans lose detail.
- Access: consent, privacy rules, and contracts can restrict use.
- Cost: collecting, cleaning, and labeling become more expensive as volume grows, especially for rare or regulated cases.

### What is Synthetic Data?
title: Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose

text:
[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-vs-real-data | Type: blog_post | Title: Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose | Published: 2026-10-23 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
[Synthetic data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-generation-platforms) is data produced by a program, model, or simulation instead of recorded from real events. It is built to follow the structure and patterns of the cases it represents, and teams use it to supply examples that are scarce, private, or costly to label.

### Strengths of Synthetic Data

- Volume on demand: examples are generated at the size a team requests.
- Rare cases: generation can target events that collected data seldom contains.
- Attached labels: generated examples can arrive with labels or completions.
- Sharing without real records: teams can share data that holds no customer or patient records.

### Limits of Synthetic Data

- Inherited assumptions: the data reflects only what the generator learned or was given.
- Repetition: generated examples can grow more repetitive as volume rises.
- Privacy obligations: personal data rules can still apply, so teams assess re-identification risk.
- Model collapse: repeated training on model output removes rare examples.

### How Do You Test Synthetic Data Against Real Data?

Test synthetic data by [training a model](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/best-platforms-to-train-ai-model-easily) on it and scoring that model on held-out real data, then compare its fidelity, coverage, diversity, and privacy risk with the real source records.

### Utility

Utility measures whether a model trained on synthetic data performs on real tasks. It is decisive because synthetic data can resemble real data statistically and still train a worse model. When you have enough real data, compare the model’s score with one trained on real data.

### Fidelity

Fidelity measures whether synthetic values and relationships resemble the real data. Compare distributions and correlations in the synthetic set with those in the real source records. This check applies mainly to structured data.

### Coverage and Diversity

Coverage and diversity measure whether synthetic data spans the topics, classes, and rare cases that real data shows, without repeating itself. Compare category frequencies with the real set, and count duplicates at the volume you plan to use, because repetition tends to grow as volume rises.

### Privacy

Privacy testing measures whether synthetic data reproduces or reveals real records. Compare synthetic records with the real source records for matches, and assess re-identification risk before sharing the data or training on it.

### Can You Combine Synthetic Data and Real Data?

Teams combine synthetic data and real data by giving each a separate job: real data anchors training and supplies the test set, and synthetic data adds coverage where real examples are thin, private, or missing.

Three patterns show how to combine them:
title: Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose

text:
[Source: https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-vs-real-data | Type: blog_post | Title: Synthetic Data vs Real Data: Differences and How to Choose | Published: 2026-10-23 | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
1. Real core, synthetic coverage. Train on collected data, then add generated examples for the rare cases and underrepresented classes the real set lacks.
2. Generation from real examples. Expand a small real set with new variations, languages, or localizations.
3. Real data in every mix. Keep a share of real data in training and monitoring, and avoid training repeatedly on a model’s own unchecked output.

### How Did AI Singapore Combine Real and Generated Data?

A one-month pilot reported in August 2026 shows generation from real examples at work. AI Singapore (AISG) and Adaption built training data for SEA-LION, AISG’s family of open-source large language models for Southeast Asian languages:

- Real source. AISG’s team sourced the real seed data.
- Generated from real examples. The Adaptive Data platform generated about 750,000 new samples by localizing those real examples, which grew coverage from seven to 11 languages and regional variants.
- Independent review. AISG’s team designed the evaluations and reviewed the outcomes.

Read the [AI Singapore pilot](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/ai-singapore-sovereign-ai-pilot) for the full results.

For generation from a small real set, teams can use [Expand Your World](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/expand-your-world), a feature of the Adaptive Data platform that scales a dataset from as few as 10 examples to up to 2,420 examples across 242 languages and localizations.

### How Do You Choose Between Synthetic Data and Real Data?

Choose based on the constraint you face. Use real data when accuracy must be checked against what happened, synthetic data when real examples are scarce, restricted, or costly to label, and both when a model needs coverage and a trustworthy test.

| Challenge                                                           | Best Choice    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Real examples are scarce                                            | Both           |
| Privacy or access rules limit real records                          | Synthetic data |
| Rare events matter, such as fraud or uncommon conditions            | Synthetic data |
| No example data exists for the behavior                             | Synthetic data |
| You need evaluation sets, reference answers, or regulated decisions | Real data      |
| You are monitoring a deployed model                                 | Real data      |

# 7 Best Platforms to Train an AI Model Easily (2026)

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Oct 28, 2026

·

5min read

The easiest way to train an AI model is to use a managed platform that handles infrastructure and training for you. Options include no-code interfaces (Hugging Face AutoTrain), fine-tuning APIs (Together AI, Replicate), cloud AI suites (Amazon Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), code-first GPU platforms (Modal), and automated training systems (AutoScientist). Choose by data, code skills, and model ownership.

### Key Takeaways

- [Fine-tuning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-continual-learning) adapts an existing model to your data, which makes it the training task most platforms automate.
- Code requirements separate these platforms: several offer browser forms or consoles, several offer APIs, and Modal runs your own Python.
- Training data is the input most platforms leave to you, so a team without a dataset must collect, label, or generate one first. Adaption offers data optimization and synthetic data generation, plus an automated training loop.
- Ownership terms differ because some platforms let you download the trained weights, and others serve the model through their own service.

### What Does It Mean to Train an AI Model Easily?

Training an AI model easily means adapting an existing model to your data without building training infrastructure or writing a training loop. This is called fine-tuning, and most teams use it instead of training from scratch, which needs a large dataset and a GPU cluster.

Four parts of the work decide how easy a platform is:

- Setup: whether you manage GPUs, containers, and drivers.
- Interface: a browser form or console, an API call, or Python code.
- Inputs: whether you bring labeled examples, preference pairs, or only a goal.
- Output: whether you can download the trained model and run it elsewhere.

No-code means you can start a training job from a browser interface without writing a script. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) is a [fine-tuning method](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails) that trains a small set of added weights, while full fine-tuning updates every weight in the model.

### What Should You Look for in a Platform for Easy AI Model Training?

Check six properties before you choose a platform: the input it needs, the code it requires, what it automates, which models it trains, who owns the output, and how it bills. Each property decides whether a team starts quickly or stalls at setup.

### Do You Need Your Own Training Data to Train an AI Model?

Most platforms [need a dataset before training starts](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails): examples that pair an input with the output you want the model to produce. A team without a dataset has three options:

- Collect and label real examples
- Optimize data they already have
- Generate a synthetic dataset

For teams limited in time or budget, or teams who don’t have any data at all, Adaption offers [Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data) and [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-invent-a-dataset). Adaptive Data is Adaption’s real-time platform that optimizes, enhances, and expands existing data. Invent a Dataset generates training-ready dataset from a description of the behavior a model should learn, with no seed data, schema, or labeling guide. Both have measured results:

- Adaptive Data platform: In a [one-month pilot reported in August 2026](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/ai-singapore-sovereign-ai-pilot), the Adaptive Data platform enhanced about 1.05 million samples of AI Singapore’s SEA-LION training data and added about 750,000 localized samples, with no human editing. The dataset grew to about 1.75 million samples and from seven to 11 languages and regional variants. AI Singapore’s team sourced the seed data and reviewed the outcomes.
- Invent a Dataset: [Adaption’s October 2026 evaluation](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/measuring-dataset-generation-abilities-with-zero-seed-data) found datasets from the Invent API, the programmatic access to Invent a Dataset, were up to 55 percent more diverse than those from frontier model APIs, with quality about 17 percent higher than the strongest baselines, at sizes from 200 to 20,000 samples.

### Can You Train an AI Model Easily With AutoScientist by Adaption?

[AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist) by Adaption makes it easier to train an AI model quickly by automating the research loop. It co-optimizes a model’s training data and training recipe against an outcome the team sets, so teams define the goal, and the system runs the experiments.

### Key Features

- Interface: A web app, a Python SDK, and a REST API. A run started from code appears in the dashboard, and a run started in the dashboard can be monitored through the API, because both show the same run.
- Starting input: A dataset you upload. AutoScientist optimizes the data as part of its loop, and Invent a Dataset can supply the dataset from a description when none exists.

# 7 Continuous Learning AI Platforms Compared

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

Oct 28, 2026

5min read

Continuous learning AI platforms keep a model current by detecting when it needs retraining, automating the retraining, and feeding it current data. Platforms differ by step: retraining triggers (Amazon SageMaker AI, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Azure Machine Learning, Databricks), model selection and tuning (H2O Driverless AI), fine-tuning of open-weight models (Hugging Face, AutoScientist), or training data (Adaptive Data platform).

## Key Takeaways

- Deployed models degrade without retraining. A 2022 [Scientific Reports study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-15245-z) of four regression model types on 32 datasets found temporal degradation in 91 percent of 128 model and dataset pairs, including datasets without abrupt changes.
- Retraining needs three working parts. The same study names a retraining trigger, an automated retraining mechanism, and constant access to recent ground truth as requirements for practical retraining.
- Drift monitoring and pipelines automate the trigger. Cloud and data platforms connect drift monitoring to retraining pipelines, so a retrain can start when measured signals change.
- Training data supply is a separate capability. It covers where each retrain’s data comes from, and platforms differ in whether they optimize, expand, or generate that data.
- Use case decides the fit. Predictive models on one cloud, open-weight fine-tuning with full control, and adapting base models to a team’s own data each point to a different platform.

### What Should You Look For in a Continuous Learning AI Platform?

Look for four capabilities in a continuous learning AI platform: a trigger that starts retraining, automation of the training itself, a steady supply of current training data, and a fit with your stack and ownership needs.

Continuous learning, also called [continual learning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-continual-learning), keeps a model current by repeatedly updating its training data and retraining as goals, domains, and inputs change. [Adaption](http://adaptionlabs.ai) is an AI company that builds continual learning systems, which let organizations train, customize, and own their AI.

Two related terms are often confused with continuous learning. Continuous training is the MLOps term for an automated pipeline that retrains a deployed model when a trigger fires. Online learning updates model weights on individual records or mini-batches as data arrives.

The need is measurable. A 2022 [Scientific Reports study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-15245-z) tested four regression model types on 32 datasets from four industries and observed temporal degradation in 91 percent of the 128 model and dataset pairs. The authors list three requirements for practical retraining: a trigger that signals when to retrain, a robust mechanism for automatic retraining, and constant access to the most recent ground truth.

1. Retraining trigger. Schedules, performance metrics, and data drift decide when a retrain starts, so check what monitoring a platform provides and what that monitoring can start.
2. Training automation. Automation can cover feature engineering and model selection, hyperparameter tuning, or the training data and training recipe together.
3. Training data supply. Each retrain learns from current data, so check whether a platform optimizes, expands, or generates that data.
4. Fit and ownership. Cloud ecosystem, model type, and who owns and deploys the resulting model decide whether a platform suits your team.

### Which Platforms Automate Retraining When a Model Drifts?

Amazon SageMaker AI, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Azure Machine Learning, and Databricks automate retraining when a model drifts by connecting drift monitoring to pipelines that run the retraining workflow.

### 1\. Amazon SageMaker AI

Amazon SageMaker AI, often shortened to SageMaker, is AWS’s managed machine learning platform. SageMaker AI Model Monitor compares live inference data with a training baseline, and SageMaker Pipelines can start a retraining workflow when drift is detected, using services such as Amazon EventBridge. It suits teams standardized on AWS.

### 2\. Azure Machine Learning

Azure Machine Learning is Microsoft’s managed machine learning platform. Model monitoring runs scheduled jobs that compute signals such as data drift on production inference data, and retraining pipelines can run on a schedule or on metrics. It suits teams building on Azure.

### 3\. Databricks

Databricks is a data and AI platform that combines data engineering, model training, managed MLflow, a feature store, model serving, and model monitoring. Lakehouse Monitoring tracks drift in input features against a baseline, and Lakeflow orchestrates pipelines from data ingestion through model deployment. It suits teams that want data engineering and machine learning on one platform.

### 4\. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Formerly Vertex AI

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI, is Google Cloud’s managed machine learning and AI platform. Model Monitoring alerts on training-serving skew and inference drift, and pipeline runs can be scheduled or triggered through Pub/Sub. It suits teams on Google Cloud.

### 1\. AutoScientist by Adaption

[AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist) by Adaption co-optimizes a model’s training data and training recipe against an outcome a team sets. It adapts base model families including Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron, Mistral, and Llama, and it suits teams that want an adapted model they own without managing hyperparameter sweeps.

Adaption’s May 2026 [evaluation of AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist) found it outperformed training configured by Adaption’s in-house AI researchers by 35 percent on average, raising win rates from 48 percent to 64 percent across eight verticals and dataset sizes from 5,000 to 100,000 samples. In a preliminary experiment reported in August 2026, AutoScientist saved AI Singapore 56 engineering hours of manual hyperparameter optimization on a small base model. A shorter loop from a new objective to a retrained model is what lets a team retrain as goals change.

### 2\. H2O Driverless AI

H2O Driverless AI is H2O.ai’s automatic machine learning platform. It automates feature engineering, model validation, tuning, selection, and deployment, and H2O MLOps monitors feature drift on deployed models for tabular data. It suits data science teams building predictive models.

### 3\. Hugging Face

Hugging Face provides open building blocks for model training. The Hub hosts models and datasets, TRL supplies trainers for supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, and Hugging Face Jobs runs a team’s training scripts on managed infrastructure. It suits teams building on open-weight models who want control over each step.

### Where Does the Training Data for Each Retrain Come From?

The [training data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data) for each retrain comes from a data supply capability, which is separate from retraining triggers and training automation and covers optimizing, expanding, and generating the examples a model learns from. Feature stores, such as those in Databricks and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, keep features consistent between training and serving. Creating and improving the examples a model learns from is a different job.

The best AI training data platform for custom model development depends on the job. Adaptive Data specializes in real-time data optimization, keeping training data current as goals change. Appen, Labelbox, and Scale AI supply expert-labeled data. Bright Data supplies web data. Databricks Mosaic AI trains custom models.

### What Is an AI Training Data Platform?

An AI training data platform is software or a service that collects, labels, generates, or optimizes the examples a model learns from. AI training data platforms fall into four types, each aimed at a different challenge:

- Human data and labeling: annotators and domain experts write, label, and rank examples. This fits teams that need expert judgment, preference data, or evaluation.
- Web and licensed data: existing data is collected and delivered, such as scraped web content or pre-collected datasets. This fits teams that need volume or fresh public information.
- Synthetic data generation: software [generates new examples from a description](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-synthetic-data) or a seed set. This fits teams where real data is scarce or private.
- Data optimization: software improves, expands, and localizes a team's own data as objectives change. This fits teams that already have data and need it to match a new goal.

In this guide, real-time data optimization means keeping the examples a model trains on aligned with current goals. It does not mean lowering the latency of a data feed.

### How Does an AI Training Data Platform Differ From a Data Platform for AI?

A data platform for AI is broader than an AI training data platform: the warehouses, lakehouses, and pipelines that store and move an organization's data for analytics and AI applications. An AI training data platform works on the examples a model learns from.

### Where Do Streaming Pipelines and Feature Stores Fit?

Real-time data pipelines move fresh operational data into the systems an AI application reads at inference. Feature stores such as Feast, an open-source feature store, and Tecton, a managed feature platform, define, store, and serve features for both model training and low-latency inference. These tools start from data a team already has. An AI training data platform creates or improves the examples that data becomes.

### What Should You Look for in an AI Training Data Platform?

Evaluate an [AI training data platform](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data) on five criteria: where the data comes from, how much control you have over it, how quality is checked, how the data updates when goals change, and the path from data to a trained model.

1. Where the data comes from. Examples can be written by people, collected from the web, generated by a model, or built from your own documents. The source determines provenance, privacy exposure, and what you can audit.
2. Control over the data. Look for the ability to [set tone, safety thresholds, content policies, domain, and languages once](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/blueprint), and have every example follow them. Weak control shows up later as brand and policy risk.
3. How quality is checked. Quality control can be human review, automated checks, or both. Ask what is measured, what happens to [examples that fail](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data), and whether a pilot can confirm the result.
4. How data updates when goals change. A dataset delivered once stays fixed. When a new objective, policy, or language arrives, the cost is a new collection cycle unless the platform re-optimizes existing data.
5. The path to a trained model. Some platforms stop at data, some export to your training stack, and some connect to training directly. This decides how many handoffs sit between your data and a model you own.

### Which AI Training Data Platform Fits Which Job?

### 1\. Adaptive Data by Adaption

[Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data) is a real-time data optimization platform that enhances, expands, and generates AI training data across 242 languages. It works with structured and unstructured data, and teams can specify behavior like length and tones. It fits best when the data exists but no longer matches the goal, or when goals change often.

### 2\. Appen

Appen's AI data platform combines automation with human oversight for data labeling, human preference scoring, LLM fine-tuning, and model evaluation, including red teaming and benchmarking. It fits best when a team needs human-generated data and evaluation in one workflow.

### 3\. Bright Data

Bright Data supplies pre-collected datasets and scraper APIs for web data, and offers annotation services in automated, hybrid, or human-supervised modes. It fits best when the bottleneck is collecting fresh public data at volume.

### 4\. Databricks Mosaic AI

Databricks Mosaic AI Model Training tunes or further trains a foundation model on a team's own data, using supervised fine-tuning or continued pre-training, with checkpoints saved to MLflow. It fits best when a team already has prepared data on Databricks and wants a custom model it owns.

### 5\. Invent a Dataset

[Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset), Adaption’s [synthetic dataset generation platform](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-generation-platforms), builds a training-ready dataset from a description of the behavior a model should learn. It requires no seed data, schema, or labeling guide. It fits best when a team has no seed data for a new task.

### 6\. Labelbox

Labelbox pairs a labeling platform with on-demand expert labeling services, and describes built-in automation and quality control. Its services cover supervised fine-tuning, multimodal LLM evaluation, and preference ranking, with expert labeling in 30+ languages. It fits best when a team wants to run labeling projects itself or with managed help.

To keep training data current as objectives change, use a platform like [Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data). A dataset delivered once stays fixed, so every new goal, policy, or language means a new collection cycle. Instead, Adaptive Data re-optimizes the data you already have. Teams specify behavior like length, tone, safety, and content policies, and an AI-written checklist removes examples that miss a requirement.

### How Do You Turn Optimized Data Into a Custom Model?

To turn optimized data into a custom model, use a platform like [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist). AutoScientist [automates the full research loop](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist) behind model training by co-optimizing the training data and training recipe against an outcome your team sets. It works across base model families including Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron, Mistral, and Llama, and the result is an adapted model your team owns.

### How Do You Choose an AI Training Data Platform by Use Case?

Choose an AI training data platform by solving for the constraint that blocks your model today: expert judgment, public web data, no data at all, data that no longer matches your goals, or the training run itself. Each constraint points to a different type of platform, and many projects combine two or three.

### Frequently Asked Questions

### Do You Need Real-Time Data to Train a Custom Model?

No. Training uses a dataset, so what matters is that the dataset matches your current objectives, not how fast a feed delivers it. Real-time pipelines matter for what a deployed model reads at inference. Real-time data optimization for training means re-optimizing the dataset whenever goals, policies, or languages change, and then retraining the model on the updated data.

### What Is the Difference Between Synthetic Data and Human-Labeled Data?

Human-labeled data is written, labeled, or ranked by people and carries their judgment. [Synthetic data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-synthetic-data) is generated by software from a description or a seed set. Human-labeled data fits expert judgment and evaluation, and synthetic data fits cases where [real data is scarce](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-vs-real-data) or private. Many teams use both and check generated data for diversity and quality before training.

# Self-Improving Intelligence for Long-Context Medical Reasoning

[Wilson Marcilio Junior](https://www.linkedin.com/in/wilson-marciliojr/)

 &

[Sudip Roy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sudip-roy-81a23b15/)

·

Oct 29, 2026

·

3min read

Wisedocs handles massive document volumes, scaling to process medical records exceeding 100,000 pages per case. Volume is also matched by complexity. In a medical record spanning a hundred visits, finding a relevant passage is critical. Tracking how a diagnosis changed, reconciling conflicting assessments or identifying every procedure requires connecting evidence scattered throughout the record.

[AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist) automatically configures AI stacks to optimize for specific use cases. Unlike most AI customization, which requires significant expertise, AutoScientist infers in a self-improving loop the best modeling choices for each task. We showcase the impact of allowing AutoScientist to auto-configure an intelligence stack by benchmarking on held-out cases from the Medical Long Context Reasoning benchmark (MLCR). AutoScientist increased correctness on MLCR from 58.1% to 75.2%, outperforming GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon and other frontier models. We also showed AutoScientist could supercharge the performance of a variety of open-weights models, with generalized gains when applied to DeepSeek and Qwen.

AutoScientist also dramatically lowers the cost profile of processing massive amounts of documents. AutoScientist applied to different open-weights models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen 3.8 27B and GLM 5.3 results in 5x to 15.4x cheaper processing versus Claude Opus 5.5\.

### How MLCR Tests Reasoning Across Long Medical Records

[MLCR](https://www.wisedocs.ai/blogs/medical-long-context-reasoning) (Medical Long Context Reasoning), built by Wisedocs, tests whether a model can reason across a long medical claim record. Each case contains 50 to 150 visit summaries, with complex questions across six difficulty tiers.

Each question is asked on the clean record and again with irrelevant medical and administrative forms interleaved at one and two filler pages per page of record, which pushes some prompts past 570,000 tokens.

Grading follows [MLCR v1.1](https://www.wisedocs.ai/blogs/mlcr-v1-1-calibrating-llm-judges-for-long-context-medical-reasoning) and is strict. An answer counts as correct only if it passes a length gate, and a three-model jury judges it both factually accurate and complete. Completeness includes the reasoning and supporting evidence the question requires.

### How a Lower-Cost Open Model Outperformed Frontier Models

Often, customization of models feels time-consuming and unpredictable. AutoScientist helps de-risk this, by automatically configuring model training and gradient-free learning techniques. For this set of experiments, we restrict AutoScientist optimization solely to optimizing and configuring everything except the model weights. This allows us to showcase how easily gains can come from applying AutoScientist to existing open weights models.

AutoScientist self-improvement was applied to three state-of-the-art open-weight models: DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen 3.8 27B and GLM 5.3\. Across the 246-question evaluation set, correctness increased in the range of 2.5 to 17.1 percentage points across these models, with the model weights unchanged.

Figure 1\. AutoScientist Improves Correctness Without Frontier Costs

AutoScientist also produced dramatic efficiency improvements. The optimized model stack brought DeepSeek V4 Flash within 4.9 percentage points of Claude Opus 5.5, the strongest model tested at 80.1%, with 15.4x cheaper processing.

AutoScientist applied to DeepSeek V4 Flash also outperformed several other frontier-model baselines that cost between 1.7 and 7.7 times as much per question.

Figure 2\. A Low-Cost Model Outperforms Frontier Models on Answer Completeness Without Retraining

The completeness pass rate rose from 76.4% to 93.9%, consistent with the evidence-coverage problem the harness targeted. Most of the overall gain came from Medium questions, which require combining facts spread across visits. Correct answers on those questions increased from 62 to 95 out of 123 evaluations, accounting for 33 of the 42 additional correct answers overall.

The searched harness was also more robust to the presence of irrelevant information. With a plain harness, adding filler forms dropped DeepSeek V4 Flash’s correct answers from 65.9% on clean records to as low as 52.4%. However, with the searched harness, it scored 75.6% on clean records and 74.4% even in the presence of a large amount of irrelevant pages.

### Better Long-Document AI Without a Bigger Model

AutoScientist enables rapid self-improvement applied to any domain, applied on top of any open weights model to drive performance and efficiency gains. Contract review, financial due diligence and technical investigations place similar demands on a model. Evidence is spread across documents, individual facts need to be connected, and an otherwise sound answer can fail because a required detail is missing.

# Most Automated Platforms for Training Custom AI Models (2026)

[Adaption Team](https://www.linkedin.com/company/adaption-labs/)

·

Nov 04, 2026

·

5min read

Platforms that automate training for a custom AI model include Adaption’s [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist), Amazon SageMaker AI, Azure Machine Learning, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, H2O Driverless AI, and Together AI. They differ in which stages they automate (infrastructure, training recipe, [training data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data), evaluation, and retraining) and in which model types they train.

### Key Takeaways

- The main difference between platforms that train a custom AI model are automation stages. A platform can automate infrastructure, the training recipe, the training data, evaluation, or retraining.
- Amazon SageMaker AI and Together AI run training for custom language models, so a team doesn’t manage the infrastructure. SageMaker AI also offers an agent-guided workflow in which a team describes a use case in natural language.
- AutoScientist, [Adaption’s](http://adaptionlabs.ai) system for automating the science behind model training, co-optimizes a model’s training data and recipe against an outcome the team sets.
- Azure Machine Learning, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and H2O Driverless AI automate model search for predictive models, such as classifiers and forecasters. Each tests many algorithms and settings on a team’s labeled data, then selects a model from the results.

### What Does Automated AI Model Training Mean?

Automated AI model training means a platform performs steps of model development that a team would otherwise do by hand. Stages that can be automated include infrastructure, training recipe, training data, evaluation, and retraining.

- Infrastructure: GPU provisioning, scaling, and job management.
- Training recipe: choosing the method, hyperparameters, and architecture.
- Training data: cleaning, [filtering](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/automated-data-quality-control-with-agentic-checklists%5C), expanding, or [generating examples](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/what-is-synthetic-data).
- Evaluation: scoring the trained model against a metric.
- Retraining: starting a new run when data or goals change.

Predictive models and language models use these stages differently. Automated machine learning (AutoML) is a set of methods that search algorithms, features, and settings to build a predictive model, such as a classifier or forecaster, from labeled records. A language model is usually adapted from a pretrained base model, which is called [fine-tuning](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails). Common methods are supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on example outputs, direct preference optimization (DPO) on preferred and rejected responses, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which trains a small adapter instead of every weight. For a language model, the training recipe and the training data decide the result.

### What Should You Look for in an Automated Training Platform?

When evaluating an automated training platform, check five criteria: the stages a platform automates, what the team still sets, the model types it trains, how it treats training data, and what output it returns.

1. Stages automated: infrastructure only, or also recipe, data, evaluation, and retraining.
2. What your team sets: settings and parameters, or the outcome you want.
3. Model types: predictive models, language models, or both.
4. Training data: whether the platform improves or [generates data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-generation-platforms), or expects a finished dataset.
5. Output: downloadable weights or a model served by the platform.

### Which Platforms Automate Training for Custom Language Models?

Adaption AutoScientist, Amazon SageMaker AI, and Together AI automate parts of adapting a language model. They differ in how much of the recipe and the data the team still handles.

### 1\. Adaption AutoScientist

[AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist), Adaption’s system for automating the science behind model training, co-optimizes a model’s training data and recipe against an outcome the team sets. AutoScientist runs recipe search, training, and evaluation across the Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron, Mistral, and Llama model families until the desired outcome is achieved. Each run ends with a checkpoint the team downloads.

Best for: teams that need a trained model quickly, don't have AI researchers on staff, or want data and training handled together, and want to own the result.

### 2\. Amazon SageMaker AI

Amazon SageMaker AI is AWS’s managed machine learning platform. Its serverless model customization trains Amazon Nova and open-weight models such as Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, and GPT-OSS with SFT, DPO, and reinforcement learning. An agent-guided workflow covers data transformation, technique selection, hyperparameter configuration, evaluation, and deployment.

Best for: teams on AWS that want guided customization of these models.

### 3\. Together AI

Together AI is a hosted platform that fine-tunes open language models with LoRA or full fine-tuning, using SFT or preference tuning. It handles data upload, training, hosting, and inference. The team supplies a prepared dataset and chooses the base model, method, and parameters.

Best for: teams with a dataset that want a managed service to train and serve an open model.

### Which Platforms Automate Training for Predictive Models?

Azure Machine Learning, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and H2O Driverless AI automate the search for a predictive model that fits labeled data. They train classifiers, regressors, and forecasters, not fine-tuned language models.

### 2\. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI, is Google Cloud’s managed AI platform. Its AutoML offers image and tabular models, and the tabular End-to-End AutoML workflow handles feature engineering, architecture search, hyperparameter tuning, and ensembling for classification and regression.

Best for: teams on Google Cloud building predictive models.

### 3\. H2O Driverless AI

H2O Driverless AI is H2O.ai’s automatic machine learning platform for supervised models. It automates feature engineering, model validation, tuning, selection, and deployment, mainly on tabular data.

Best for: data science teams building predictive models.

### Which Platforms Automate the Training Data Stage?

Platforms that automate the training data stage include Amazon SageMaker AI and Adaption. Adaption offers the most robust training data of the two. Azure Machine Learning, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, H2O Driverless AI, and Together AI expect the team to supply a prepared dataset.

### Adaption

[Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data), Adaption’s real-time data optimization platform, enhances, expands, and generates AI training data across 242 languages and localizations. A team uses it to improve a dataset it already has. [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset), Adaption’s dataset generation platform, builds a training-ready dataset from a plain language description of the behavior a model should learn.

AutoScientist trains on either dataset and adds data during training to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and lack of diversity. A team with no training data can generate a dataset, train on it, and end up with a model it owns.

### Amazon SageMaker AI

Amazon SageMaker AI uses a coding agent to format a team’s data and validate its quality.

Yes. Azure Machine Learning has a studio for automated ML, Amazon SageMaker AI has a guided interface in SageMaker Studio, and Together AI has a console for launching fine-tuning jobs. AutoScientist has a dashboard, [an API, and an SDK](https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/autoscientist/overview/), so a team can set an outcome without writing a training loop.

### Does Automated Training Remove the Need to Evaluate the Model?

No. Automated training selects and trains candidates against a metric or outcome that a team defines, so the result is only as good as that definition. Human judgment still guides goals and evaluation.

### What Is the Difference Between AutoML and Automated Language Model Training?

AutoML searches algorithms, features, and hyperparameters to build a predictive model from labeled records. Automated language model training adapts a pretrained base model, so the training data and the training recipe decide the result. The two categories automate different stages.

### How Long Does Automated Training Take?

Training time depends on model size, dataset size, hardware, and the number of experiments needed to find a working recipe. AutoScientist automates those experiments, and makes it possible to own a custom model in days or weeks.

### What Is Training Co-Optimization?

Training co-optimization is the automated, simultaneous tuning of a model’s training data and training recipe, so each improves in light of the other instead of being tuned separately. AutoScientist iterates on both together until performance converges on the outcome the team sets, and it adds data during training to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and a lack of diversity.

[Adaption](http://adaptionlabs.ai) AutoScientist, Hugging Face TRL, Databricks Mosaic AI Model Training, and Together AI give you the most direct ownership. ### Key Takeaways

- Downloadable weights are the primary test of whether a platform lets a team own an AI model. A team that holds the weights can run the model on another host without retraining.
- Training data rights limit what an owned AI model can be used for. Some frontier model providers do not permit training on data generated with their models, so a dataset built from their outputs can restrict the resulting model. A team should read each provider’s terms before training.
- Base model licenses can follow an owned AI model that was [fine-tuned](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails) from an open-weight base model. The derived weights can carry the base model’s terms, so a team that holds the weights should confirm what the license allows before the model ships.
- Owned AI model training can be automated. [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist), Adaption’s system for automating the science behind model training, co-optimizes a model’s training data and training recipe against an outcome the team sets, and each run ends with a checkpoint the team can download.
- [Synthetic data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/synthetic-data-generation-platforms) lets healthcare, finance, legal, and other regulated teams build an owned AI model when real customer records cannot go into training. ### What Does It Mean to Own an AI Model?

Owning an AI model means your organization holds the trained weights and can run, change, and move the model without asking a provider. Ownership has four layers, and a platform can give you some and withhold others.

- Weights. You hold the trained parameters, or the adapter that modifies a base model. Ask whether you can download them or the platform only serves them.
- [Training data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data). You hold the dataset and the right to train on it. Ask whether the data’s terms allow commercial training.
- Recipe. You can reproduce the training with the same data and settings. Ask whether the configuration and evaluation are yours to keep.
- Deployment. You choose where the model runs. Ask whether it can run on your hardware or another host.

The platforms in this guide build models you control. Legal research and drafting applications are a different product, because you license them. Many teams use both, with an application for common work and a custom model where the firm’s workflow, data, or confidentiality needs are specific.

[Adaption](http://adaptionlabs.ai), Applied Compute, Baseten, Fireworks AI, Hugging Face, Thinking Machines, and Trajectory answer both differently. Some give you raw tools and expect you to write the code. Others run the whole loop for you.

### Key Takeaways

- The training loop is the biggest difference. Adaption runs an automated four-stage loop against a target win rate you set. Baseten, Hugging Face, and Thinking Machines supply the GPUs and leave defining all of the training configuration up to you. Fireworks AI runs managed jobs on your dataset.
- Training data comes from a different place on each platform. [Baseten](https://www.baseten.co/), [Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai/), [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/), and [Thinking Machines](https://thinkingmachines.ai/) leave preparing the dataset to the user. [Applied Compute](https://www.appliedcompute.com/) and [Trajectory](https://www.trajectory.ai/) build data from production use, but are not self-serve and don’t have an api available for everyday developers. Adaption can optimize your raw data or generate synthetic data before training.
- Training methods vary. Adaption’s system [runs SFT and DPO](https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/autoscientist/supported-models/), and Applied Compute and Trajectory center on reinforcement learning. Fireworks AI, Hugging Face, and Thinking Machines support both. Baseten runs whatever code you bring.
- A no-data path exists at Adaption. If you need to fine-tune a model but don’t have any data, [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset) generates an AI-ready training dataset from a plain language description. There is an api available for everyday developers.

### What Does a Fine-Tuning Platform Do?

A [fine-tuning](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/what-is-fine-tuning/) platform trains an existing AI model on your examples, so it follows your task, format, or domain more reliably than prompting a generic model alone. [Training adjusts the model’s weights](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/why-fine-tuning-fails), and platforms differ in two choices: what the model learns from, and how much it changes.

What the model learns from:

- Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains a model on example inputs paired with the outputs you want.
- Direct preference optimization (DPO) trains on pairs of preferred and rejected responses.
- Reinforcement learning (RL) trains against scores from a grader. You need a way to judge outcomes, not example answers.

How much of the model changes:

- LoRA trains a small adapter on top of frozen weights.
- Full fine-tuning updates every weight and costs more compute.

### How Should You Evaluate a Fine-Tuning Platform?

Judge a fine-tuning platform on five criteria: who runs the training loop, where the [training data comes from](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/best-ai-training-data-platforms), which training methods it supports, what you get after training, and what you own.

1. Who runs the training loop. Writing the training loop yourself gives you control over the algorithm, but requires specialized expertise and costs engineering time. Managed jobs and automated systems give up some control for speed.
2. Where the training data comes from. Every platform [needs a dataset ](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/true-cost-of-bad-training-data)before it can train. Some expect you to bring a cleaned, formatted dataset. Others help you prepare, expand, or generate it. That choice sets how soon your first run can start and how much data work your team does.
3. Which training methods it supports. SFT and DPO fit tasks where you have example outputs or preferred answers. RL fits tasks where you can score a result but can’t write the correct answer, such as an agent finishing a multistep job. Match the method to your task before you compare platforms.
4. What you get after training. Platforms return different things: a checkpoint (a saved copy of the trained weights), a hosted model, or both. A checkpoint alone means you set up serving yourself. A hosted model means the platform runs it for you.
5. What you own. Some platforms let you download the trained weights and serve them anywhere. Others keep the model on their own infrastructure. If you can’t take the weights with you, switching platforms later means retraining.

### How Do the Seven Fine-Tuning Platforms Compare?

The seven platforms fall into three groups:

- Adaption [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist) runs the end-to-end model training loop and alignment.
- Baseten, Fireworks AI, Hugging Face, and Thinking Machines supply the infrastructure, and you write or configure the training run.
- Applied Compute and Trajectory build the model, either alongside your team or from your production feedback.

Best for: teams with a product in production and domain experts whose corrections can serve as the training signal.

Three of the seven platforms create or improve training data: Adaption, Applied Compute, and Trajectory. You need to provide training-ready data to train a model with Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Thinking Machines.

- Applied Compute: builds data pipelines with customers in AC2, including task queries generated by prompting frontier models.
- Trajectory: builds training data from production traces, edits, and expert corrections.

### What Is the Best AI Platform for Healthcare?

No single platform fits every healthcare use. ### What Is Fine-Tuning in Healthcare AI?

Fine-tuning is additional training of a pretrained model on task-specific examples, which changes the model's weights so it performs better on that task. In healthcare, the examples might be visit-note summaries or referral classifications. Prompt engineering is often tried first, and fine-tuning fits when prompts alone do not reach the quality a task needs.

Today we introduce Expand, a new feature in [Adaptive Data](https://adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data), which allows you to go from a handful of examples of the capability you care about, to a large scale training dataset. Start with 10 examples, and in a few clicks expand to 100,000 data points similar to your tasks and optimized for AI training.

### Expand Adds Examples Your Data Is Missing

Models trained on too few examples often fail on phrasing and situations they haven’t seen. This can lead to hallucinations or inaccurate answers. Expand generates the additional examples a model needs to respond to variation, and supercharge your enterprise context.

If you’re training a model to handle medical insurance claims questions, and you have a few thousand reviewed claims, Expand can grow your dataset in three ways.

1. Add more data like yours. Expand generates synthetic examples in the style of your own data. It samples your examples and closely matches their topics, language, and format. If your data has claim summaries, Expand writes more, across different damage types, amounts, and phrasing.
2. Add related tasks from your domain. Expand adds other tasks within the same domain. For example, other tasks in the medical field. This builds model robustness, so fewer tasks are unfamiliar to your model.
3. Add other domains for optimal training balance. Training quality improves when the data is varied. Turning this on activates a data agent that picks the mix of topics and sources that will maximize performance on your task.

Expand sits alongside [Translate and Localize](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/expand-your-world) in Adaptive Data. Translate carries your dataset into up to 242 languages, and Localize matches it to a specific language and country, so your model serves every market you work in.

### From Dataset to Frontier Model

Model quality is limited by how closely your data matches the objective you want. Expand brings your data closer to that objective, and [AutoScientist](https://adaptionlabs.ai/auto-scientist) carries it the rest of the way. Bring your expanded dataset into AutoScientist, and it optimizes your data and training recipe together on the open weights model you choose. That cuts the time to a high-performing model from weeks to days.

Expand joins [Invent a Dataset](https://adaptionlabs.ai/invent-a-dataset) as a starting point on the path to a custom model. Invent a Dataset starts from a description when you have no examples at all. Expand starts from the examples you already have, however few. Either way, you end up in the same place: a model trained on your knowledge, fitted to your goal, and owned by your team.

[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data-quickstart/ | Type: docs | Title: Adaptive Data quickstart | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
# Adaptive Data quickstart

> Install the Adaption Python SDK, import data, run Adaptive Data, and download the adapted dataset.

## Install the SDK

Terminal window

```
pip install adaption
```

## Create an API key

1. [Sign in](https://adaptionlabs.ai/app/auth) to Adaption.

2. Open [**Settings**](https://adaptionlabs.ai/app/settings), then open [**API keys**](https://adaptionlabs.ai/app/settings?tab=api_keys).

3. Create a key and copy it. You will not be able to view the key again.

Store API keys in environment variables or a secret manager. Do not commit them to source control.

## Use the key in Python

For local testing, you can pass the key directly:

```
from adaption import Adaption

client = Adaption(api_key="pt_live_...")
```

For applications and CI, set `ADAPTION_API_KEY`:

Terminal window

```
export ADAPTION_API_KEY="pt_live_..."
```

The SDK reads the environment variable automatically:

```
from adaption import Adaption

client = Adaption()
```

## Create a dataset

This quickstart [imports the Alpaca dataset from Hugging Face](/adaptive-data/create-a-dataset/index.md):

```
dataset = client.datasets.create(
    source={
        "url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/tatsu-lab/alpaca",
        "files": [
            "data/train-00000-of-00001-a09b74b3ef9c3b56.parquet"
        ],
    },
)
dataset_id = dataset.dataset_id
print(dataset_id)
```

You can upload a local file or import from Kaggle instead. Each source uses the same [`datasets.create`](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/create/index.md) endpoint and returns the `dataset_id` used by the rest of this guide.

Upload a local file

The SDK helper creates the dataset, uploads the file, and confirms the upload.

Supported extensions: **`.csv`**, **`.json`**, **`.jsonl`**, and **`.parquet`**.

```
dataset = client.datasets.upload_file("training_data.csv")
dataset_id = dataset.dataset_id
print(dataset_id)
```

Import from Kaggle

Use the Kaggle dataset page URL and the files to pull.

```
dataset = client.datasets.create(
    source={
        "url": "https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/sms-spam-collection-dataset",
        "files": ["spam.csv"],
    },
)
dataset_id = dataset.dataset_id
print(dataset_id)
```

**Kaggle credentials** must be registered in Adaption: open **[API keys settings](https://adaptionlabs.ai/app/settings?tab=api_keys)** (sign in if prompted) and add your Kaggle API credentials there before importing.

[Imports run asynchronously](/adaptive-data/create-a-dataset#wait-for-the-import/index.md). Wait until ingestion has populated the dataset before starting Adaptive Data.

## Wait for the dataset to import

Poll the [dataset status](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/get_status/index.md) until the imported row count is available:

```
import time
title: Adaptive Data quickstart

text:
[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data-quickstart/ | Type: docs | Title: Adaptive Data quickstart | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
while True:
    status = client.datasets.get_status(dataset_id)
    if status.status == "failed":
        err = status.error_data
        msg = (err and err.message) or "unknown error"
        raise RuntimeError(f"Ingestion failed: {msg}")
    if status.row_count is not None:
        print(f"Imported {status.row_count} rows")
        break
    time.sleep(5)
```

## Adapt the dataset

**Adapt** applies the platform’s recipes and optimizations. [Map the source columns](/adaptive-data/select-columns/index.md) to the roles Adaptive Data expects. For Alpaca, `instruction` is the prompt, `output` is the completion, and `input` is context.

[Request an estimate first](/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data#limit-rows-and-estimate-a-run/index.md). This validates the configuration and returns a quote without starting the run:

```
column_mapping = {
    "prompt": "instruction",
    "completion": "output",
    "context": ["input"],
}
job_specification = {"max_rows": 5_000}

estimate = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    job_specification=job_specification,
    estimate=True,
)
print(f"Estimated credits: {estimate.estimated_credits_consumed}")
```

When you are ready to proceed, submit the same configuration without `estimate=True`:

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    job_specification=job_specification,
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

## Wait for Adaptive Data completion

The SDK helper polls the [dataset status](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/get_status/index.md) until the adaptation run finishes:

```
status = client.datasets.wait_for_completion(dataset_id, timeout=3600)
if status.status == "failed":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Adaptive Data failed: {status.error_data}")

print(status.status)
```

## Download the adapted dataset

**Export** augmented data for training pipelines, evaluation harnesses, or downstream storage. [`download`](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/download/index.md) streams the processed rows in the requested file format. It accepts a `file_format` argument of `csv`, `json`, `jsonl`, or `parquet`, and defaults to `csv`.

```
client.datasets.download(dataset_id, file_format="parquet").write_to_file(
    "adapted-alpaca.tar.gz"
)
```

`download` returns the file itself, not a link to it. Read the bytes with `.read()`, write them straight to disk with `.write_to_file(path)`, or decode a text format with `.text()` — a method, not a property. This shape requires `adaption >= 0.9.0`; earlier releases returned a string and corrupted every binary format.

For large exports, stream instead of holding the body in memory:

```
with client.datasets.with_streaming_response.download(
    dataset_id, file_format="parquet"
) as export:
    export.stream_to_file("adapted-alpaca.tar.gz")
```

`file_format="parquet"` returns a **gzipped tar archive of Parquet shards**, not a single `.parquet` file — extract it before reading:
title: Adaptive Data quickstart

text:
[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data-quickstart/ | Type: docs | Title: Adaptive Data quickstart | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
```
import tarfile

with tarfile.open("adapted-alpaca.tar.gz") as archive:
    archive.extractall("adapted-alpaca/")
```

A dataset with status **`succeeded`** contains the full output. For a **`failed`** dataset, the download contains rows processed before the run stopped; the API returns `422` only if no run has started.

## Going further

- [AutoScientist quickstart](/autoscientist-quickstart/index.md) — train a model from your adapted dataset.
- [Configure Adaptive Data](/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data/index.md) — limit rows, reduce hallucinations, generate reasoning traces, and apply brand controls.
- [Evaluating dataset quality](/adaptive-data/evaluate-dataset-quality/index.md) — inspect evaluation status and metrics.
- [Processing unstructured documents](/runbooks/processing-unstructured-documents/index.md) — prepare document-style data.
- Browse the [API reference](/api/python/index.md) for full method signatures and response schemas.

[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/combine-datasets/ | Type: docs | Title: Combine datasets | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
# Combine datasets

> Validate and merge multiple Adaptive Data datasets into one new dataset with the Python SDK.

Combine datasets when related training examples are spread across multiple Adaptive Data results. Combining creates a new dataset and leaves every source dataset unchanged.

Each source must belong to your organization and have completed an Adaptive Data run. The examples assume you have [configured the Python SDK](/introduction/getting-started/index.md).

## Validate the source datasets

Validate the datasets before combining them. Validation checks compatibility without writing data:

```
from adaption import Adaption

client = Adaption()

dataset_ids = [
    "dataset_abc123",
    "dataset_def456",
]

validation = client.datasets.combine.validate(dataset_ids=dataset_ids)

for issue in validation.issues:
    print(issue.level, issue.code, issue.message)

if not validation.compatible:
    raise ValueError("The datasets cannot be combined")

print(validation.training_type, validation.total_estimated_rows)
```

Each validation issue has a `level`, stable `code`, and user-facing `message`:

- **Errors** block the combine. For example, a source might not be ready, might belong to another organization, or might mix text and multimodal data.
- **Warnings** describe changes the combine operation can make automatically. It can cast mismatched column types to a common type or resolve mixed training types to an instruction dataset.

See the [`combine.validate` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/subresources/combine/methods/validate/index.md) for all validation fields and issue codes.

## Combine the datasets

Pass the same source IDs to `combine.create` and give the output dataset a name:

```
from uuid import uuid4

idempotency_key = str(uuid4())

combined = client.datasets.combine.create(
    dataset_ids=dataset_ids,
    name="Combined support data",
    idempotency_key=idempotency_key,
)

print(combined.dataset_id)
```

The request runs synchronously and returns the new `dataset_id` after the merge finishes. There is no public combine-job polling flow.

Keep the same `idempotency_key` if you retry the request. A retry with that key returns the dataset created by the first request instead of starting another merge. The key is optional, but supplying one is useful if a long-running request loses its connection.

Datasets with the same training type preserve that type. Combining instruction and preference datasets produces an instruction dataset. Other warning-level reconciliation is reported by validation before you start the merge.

See the [`combine.create` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/subresources/combine/methods/create/index.md) for current request requirements and response fields.
title: Combine datasets

[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data/ | Type: docs | Title: Configure Adaptive Data | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
# Configure Adaptive Data

> Generate instruction or preference data, apply recipes, limit rows, and control adapted outputs.

After you [map your columns](/adaptive-data/select-columns/index.md), configure how Adaptive Data transforms them. You can choose its training format, apply recipes, limit the run, and define output requirements.

The SDK examples below assume you have [configured the Python SDK](/introduction/getting-started/index.md) and set `ADAPTION_DATASET_ID` to an [imported dataset](/adaptive-data/create-a-dataset/index.md):

```
import os

from adaption import Adaption

client = Adaption()
dataset_id = os.environ["ADAPTION_DATASET_ID"]
column_mapping = {
    "prompt": "instruction",
    "completion": "response",
}
```

## How a run is processed

A run always applies your settings in the same order. This means the order you pass your arguments to `datasets.adapt` has no effect.

1. **Map columns.** `column_mapping` selects which source columns are read as the prompt, completion, chat, and context.

2. **Limit rows.** If `job_specification.max_rows` is set, a sample of that many rows is selected: a random sample for text datasets, the first rows for image datasets. Later steps see only those rows.

3. **Deduplicate.** Exact duplicate rows are removed. This happens after sampling, so a run with `max_rows=500` can return fewer than 500 rows.

4. **Expand languages.** If `translate` or `localize` is set, a share of the remaining rows is copied into each target language or locale and added as new rows. Expansion comes before rephrasing and generation, so translated rows are rephrased and completed in their target language. The completions are written in that language, not translated afterwards.

5. **Rephrase prompts.** If `prompt_rephrase` is on, each prompt is rewritten, including the prompts on rows added in step 4. Datasets mapped through a `chat` column are not rephrased. `length` is applied here as guidance attached to the rewritten prompt, so it takes effect only when `prompt_rephrase` is on.

6. **Generate completions.** Each row receives its adapted completion. `training_type` decides what this step produces: one completion for `instruction_dataset`, or a chosen and rejected pair for `preference_pairs`. Two brand controls apply here:

   - `blueprint` is given to the model as a system instruction.
   - `hallucination_mitigation` runs a web search first, for prompts that need current information, and passes the results to the model. It applies to text datasets only.

7. **Capture reasoning traces.** If `reasoning_traces` is on, every row is completed by reasoning models and the reasoning behind each completion is saved as it is generated. It is not a separate pass over the data.

8. **Review safety.** If `safety_categories` is set, each finished completion is reviewed after generation.
title: Configure Adaptive Data

text:
[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data/ | Type: docs | Title: Configure Adaptive Data | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
Credits are estimated from your row limit plus the rows `translate` and `localize` will add, so they raise the estimate even when `max_rows` stays the same. Rows from `expand` are priced separately and included in the same estimate. Duplicates are not known in advance, so the final row count can be lower than the estimate. Use `estimate=True` to see the figure before you start the run.

## Apply recipes

Recipes are optional transformations that operate on the mapped data:

- **Prompt deduplication** removes duplicate prompts to keep examples diverse.
- **Prompt rephrasing** rewrites prompts for clarity and alignment with the task.
- **Reasoning traces** provides associated reasoning for adapted completions.

In the SDK, recipes belong under `recipe_specification.recipes`. You can enable more than one recipe in the same run:

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    recipe_specification={
        "recipes": {
            "deduplication": True,
            "prompt_rephrase": True,
            "reasoning_traces": True,
        },
    },
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

The exact reasoning-trace output depends on the API and recipe version. Inspect the downloaded dataset and see `RecipeSpecification` on the [`datasets.adapt` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/adapt/index.md).

Use reasoning traces if you want to fine-tune a model that supports chain-of-thought reasoning.

## Generate preference pairs

By default, Adaptive Data produces an instruction dataset for supervised fine-tuning. Set `training_type` to `preference_pairs` when you instead need chosen and rejected responses for preference training such as DPO.

The source mapping stays the same: provide a `prompt` column and, optionally, an existing `completion` column. Adaptive Data generates the preference-pair fields in the output.

```
preference_mapping = {
    "prompt": "instruction",
    "completion": "response",
}

estimate = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=preference_mapping,
    training_type="preference_pairs",
    estimate=True,
)
print(f"Estimated credits: {estimate.estimated_credits_consumed}")

run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=preference_mapping,
    training_type="preference_pairs",
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

Use `training_type="instruction_dataset"`—or omit `training_type`—to produce enhanced prompt/completion pairs instead. Language expansion, recipes, job limits, and brand controls can be included in the same preference-pair run. See `training_type` on the [`datasets.adapt` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/adapt/index.md) for the current schema.

## Add rows and languages to a run

`datasets.adapt` can grow the dataset in the same run:
title: Configure Adaptive Data

text:
[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data/ | Type: docs | Title: Configure Adaptive Data | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
- `translate` adds a translated copy of a share of the rows for each target language.
- `localize` adds a copy localized to each country and language pair.
- `expand` adds new rows before adaptation starts: `similar_rows` generated in the style of your dataset, `domain_rows` retrieved from topics that match it, and `general_rows` retrieved from other topics to broaden it.

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    translate={
        "languages": ["es", "fr"],
        "sample_rate": 0.25,
    },
    localize={
        "pairs": [{"country": "ES", "language": "ca"}],
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
    },
    expand={
        "similar_rows": 500,
        "general_rows": 1000,
    },
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

Passing any of `translate`, `localize` or `expand` sets the whole selection for the run: a field you leave out is turned off, including one chosen in the app. With none of them, the run uses the selection saved on the dataset.

The rows Expand adds are adapted together with your own rows. Translation and localization apply only to your own rows. Each Expand block costs 1 credit per 100 rows, rounded up, on top of the adaptation. Set at least one count above `0`; each is capped at `100,000`. Expand returns `400` when it is not enabled for your organization or when the dataset has image context.

`language_expansion` is deprecated. It holds one language mode at a time and cannot be combined with these fields. Requests that already use it keep working.

## Limit rows and estimate a run

Use `job_specification.max_rows` to test mappings and controls on a subset before processing a large dataset. [Request an estimate with `datasets.adapt`](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/adapt/index.md) first to validate the same configuration and receive a credit quote without starting adaptation:

```
job_specification = {"max_rows": 500}

estimate = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    job_specification=job_specification,
    estimate=True,
)
print(f"Estimated credits: {estimate.estimated_credits_consumed}")

run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    job_specification=job_specification,
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

Omit `max_rows` when you want to process the full dataset. See `JobSpecification` on the [`datasets.adapt` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/adapt/index.md) for all job-level options.

## Configure brand controls

`brand_controls` makes output requirements part of the adaptation run:

- **`length`** controls target verbosity: `minimal`, `concise`, `detailed`, or `extensive`.
- **`safety_categories`** identifies content-safety categories to enforce.
- **`hallucination_mitigation`** grounds generations with web search where applicable.
- **`blueprint`** supplies freeform instructions for tone, persona, audience, language, or product-specific wording.

### Reduce hallucinations
title: Configure Adaptive Data

text:
[Source: https://docs.adaptionlabs.ai/adaptive-data/configure-adaptive-data/ | Type: docs | Title: Configure Adaptive Data | Published: unknown | Retrieved: 2026-11-17]
Hallucination mitigation steers generated completions toward verifiable information. Enable it for fact-sensitive data such as customer support, grounded question answering, or compliance workflows:

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    brand_controls={"hallucination_mitigation": True},
)
```

Grounding can affect latency and credit use. Use `estimate=True` to compare the run before scaling it.

### Control length and safety

Length and safety constraints compose in the same `brand_controls` object. Use the [`datasets.adapt` reference](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/adapt/index.md) as the source of truth for supported safety category names:

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    brand_controls={
        "length": "concise",
        "safety_categories": ["harassment", "hate"],
    },
)
```

### Set a Blueprint

Use `blueprint` for qualitative requirements that do not fit a structured field. It acts as a system instruction for generated completions and applies consistently across the run:

```
run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    brand_controls={
        "blueprint": (
            "You are a customer-success assistant for Acme. "
            "Answer in British English with a warm, direct tone. "
            "Do not recommend third-party tools."
        ),
    },
)
```

### Combine brand controls

Structured controls and Blueprint instructions can be used together:

```
brand_controls = {
    "length": "concise",
    "safety_categories": ["harassment", "hate"],
    "hallucination_mitigation": True,
    "blueprint": "Answer in British English with a warm, direct tone.",
}

estimate = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    brand_controls=brand_controls,
    job_specification={"max_rows": 500},
    estimate=True,
)
print(f"Estimated credits: {estimate.estimated_credits_consumed}")

run = client.datasets.adapt(
    dataset_id,
    column_mapping=column_mapping,
    brand_controls=brand_controls,
    job_specification={"max_rows": 500},
)
print(f"Run started: {run.run_id}")
```

After the run completes, [evaluate dataset quality](/adaptive-data/evaluate-dataset-quality/index.md) and [download the adapted rows](/api/python/resources/datasets/methods/download/index.md).
title: Configure Adaptive Data

text:

# Create a dataset

The examples assume you have [installed the Python SDK and set `ADAPTION_API_KEY`](/introduction/getting-started/index.md):


Supported extensions: **`.csv`**, **`.json`**, **`.jsonl`**, and **`.parquet`**. Documents (**`.pdf`**, **`.docx`**, **`.pptx`**, **`.xlsx`**, **`.html`**, **`.txt`**, and **`.zip`**) upload the same way but need an extraction step first; see [Upload documents](#upload-documents).

```
dataset = client.datasets.upload_file("training_data.csv")
dataset_id = dataset.dataset_id
```

2\. Import from Hugging Face

```
dataset = client.datasets.create(

        "url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/tatsu-lab/alpaca",
        "files": [
            "data/train-00000-of-00001-a09b74b3ef9c3b56.parquet"
        ],
    },
)
dataset_id = dataset.dataset_id
print(dataset_id)
```

3\. Import from Kaggle

Use the Kaggle dataset page URL and the files to pull.

```
dataset = client.datasets.create(
    source={
        "url": "https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/sms-spam-collection-dataset",

    },
```
